entries.zh: 本注曰：主簿录阁下事，省文书。
entries.en: The chief clerk managed office business under the colonel and vetted correspondence.
entries.literal: Original note says: The chief clerk records affairs below the gate tower and examines documents.

entries.zh: 门亭长主州正。
entries.en: The gate chief enforced provincial discipline at headquarters.
entries.literal: Gate pavilion chief is in charge of provincial rectification.

entries.zh: 门功曹书佐主选用。
entries.en: The merit clerk's aide handled personnel selection.
entries.literal: Gate merit bureau document assistant is in charge of selection and appointment.

entries.zh: 《孝经》师主监试经。
entries.en: The Classic of Filial Piety instructor supervised classical examinations.
entries.literal: Master of the Classic of Filial Piety is in charge of supervising examination of the classics.

entries.zh: 《月令》师主时节祠祀。
entries.en: The Monthly Ordinances specialist oversaw seasonal temple rites.
entries.literal: Master of the Monthly Ordinances is in charge of seasonal sacrifices.

entries.zh: 律令师主平法律。
entries.en: The statute specialist advised on legal interpretation.
entries.literal: Master of statutes and ordinances is in charge of leveling the laws.

entries.zh: 簿曹书佐主簿书。
entries.en: The accounts clerk's aide kept the ledgers.
entries.literal: Ledger bureau document assistant is in charge of ledgers and documents.

entries.zh: 其余都官书佐及每郡国，各有典郡书佐一人，各主一郡文书，以郡吏补，岁满一更。
entries.en: Each commandery also supplied a resident clerk for its documents, rotated annually from local officials.
entries.literal: As for the remaining capital bureau document assistants and for each commandery and kingdom, each has one commandery classic document assistant, each in charge of one commandery's documents; they are filled from commandery clerks; when the year is full, one rotation.

entries.zh: 司隶所部郡七。
entries.en: The colonel director of retainers oversaw seven commanderies.
entries.literal: The colonel director of retainers' department commanderies are seven.

entries.zh: 右属北军中候。
entries.en: These five colonels answered to the northern-army middle commandant.
entries.literal: Those on the right belong to the middle commandant of the northern army.

entries.zh: 本注曰：旧有中垒校尉，领北军营垒之事。
entries.en: Formerly a colonel of the central bastion had overseen the northern camps' fortifications.
entries.literal: Original note says: Formerly there was a colonel of the central rampart, in charge of northern army camp rampart affairs.

entries.zh: 有胡骑、虎贲校尉，皆武帝置。
entries.en: Emperor Wu had also created separate Hu-cavalry and tiger-rushers colonels.
entries.literal: There were colonels of Hu cavalry and tiger-rushers; all were established by Emperor Wu.

entries.zh: 中兴省中垒，但置中候，以监五营。
entries.en: The restored Han abolished the central bastion colonel and used only the middle commandant to supervise the five camps.
entries.literal: At the restoration the central rampart was abolished; only the middle commandant was established, in order to supervise the five camps.

entries.zh: 胡骑并长水。
entries.en: The Hu-cavalry colonelcy was merged into the Long Water command.
entries.literal: Hu cavalry was merged into long-water.

entries.zh: 虎贲主轻车，并射声。
entries.en: The tiger-rushers' light chariots were folded into the hidden-archers regiment.
entries.literal: Tiger-rushers were in charge of light chariots; merged into sounding-the-shot.

entries.zh: 志第二十七 百官四
entries.en: Treatise 27: The Bureaucracy, Part Four.
entries.literal: Treatise twenty-seven: Officials, part four.

entries.zh: 中二千石、二千石皆皁蓋，朱兩轓。
entries.en: Officials at full and straight two thousand piculs used black canopies with red both-side sashes.
entries.literal: Fully two thousand piculs and two thousand piculs all had black canopies and vermillion on both screen-bars.

entries.zh: 其千石、六百石，朱左轓。
entries.en: One-thousand- and six-hundred-picul ranks kept red only on the left sash.
entries.literal: Those at one thousand and six hundred piculs had vermillion on the left screen-bar only.

entries.zh: 轓長六尺，下屈廣八寸，上業廣尺二寸，九文，十二初，後謙一寸，若月初生，示不敢自滿也。
entries.en: Each sash was six feet long, eight inches across the lower flare, twelve inches at the crown, cut with nine motifs and twelve scallops, the trailing edge pared back an inch like a crescent moon to signal humility.
entries.literal: The screen-bar was six chi long; the lower bend was eight cun wide; the upper head was one chi two cun wide, nine patterns, twelve notches, the rear modest one cun, like the new moon, showing not daring to be full of oneself.

entries.zh: 景帝中元五年，始詔六百石以上施車轓，得銅五末，軛有吉陽筩。
entries.en: In Jing’s Zhongyuan 5 an edict allowed six-hundred-picul officials and above to mount carriage sashes, bronze tips on fittings, and lucky tubes on the yoke.
entries.literal: In the fifth year of Emperor Jing’s middle era he first ordered that from six hundred piculs upward carriage screen-bars be applied, could use bronze on the five extremities, and the yoke had auspicious tubes.

entries.zh: 中二千石以上右騑，三百石以上皁布蓋，千石以上皁繒覆蓋，二百石以下白布蓋，皆有四維槓衣。
entries.en: Two-thousand-picul ranks added a right trace; three hundred and up used black cloth canopies; one thousand and up had black silk overlay; below two hundred, white cloth—all with corner ties and wrapped poles.
entries.literal: From fully two thousand piculs upward there was a right trace horse; from three hundred piculs upward black cloth canopy; from one thousand piculs upward black silk covering canopy; from two hundred piculs downward white cloth canopy; all had four-cornered tie-ropes and pole cloths.

entries.zh: 賈人不得乘馬車。
entries.en: Traders were forbidden horse-drawn passenger carriages.
entries.literal: Merchants were not permitted to ride horse-drawn carriages.

entries.zh: 除吏赤畫槓，其餘皆青雲。
entries.en: Retired officers kept crimson-wrapped shafts; everyone else used blue cloud designs.
entries.literal: Dismissed officials had red-painted pole cloths; the rest all had blue cloud pattern.

entries.zh: 《書》曰：「明試以功，車服以庸。」
entries.en: The Classic of Documents declares: “Prove their worth by what they achieve, then reward merit with the carriages and vestments befitting it.”
entries.literal: The Documents says: “Clearly test them by their deeds; grant chariots and robes according to their merit.”

entries.zh: 言昔者聖人興天下之大利，除天下之大害，躬親其事，身履其勤，憂之勞之，不避寒暑，使天下之民物，各得安其性命，無夭昏暴陵之災。
entries.en: The sense is this: the ancient sage labored for the common good of the realm and swept away its gravest evils—taking the burden on his own shoulders, braving every season, until every living thing could keep its natural span free from untimely death, tyranny, or plunder.
entries.literal: It means that in antiquity the sage raised the great benefits for all under Heaven and removed the great harms for all under Heaven; he personally undertook the task, himself endured the toil, worried and labored over it, did not shun cold or heat, and caused the people and creatures of the world each to secure their lives and persons without the disasters of premature death, violence, or oppression.

entries.zh: 是以天下之民，敬而愛之，若親父母；
entries.en: So the folk revered and cherished him as they would their own parents;
entries.literal: Therefore the people of the world revered and loved him as if he were father and mother;

entries.zh: 則而養之，若仰日月。
entries.en: they took his example for their nurture, as one lifts the face toward sun and moon.
entries.literal: they took him as their model and nurtured him as if gazing up at sun and moon.

entries.zh: 夫愛之者欲其長久，不憚力役，相與起作宮室，上棟下宇，以雍覆之，欲其長久也；
entries.en: Love made them wish him to endure forever, so they shouldered corvée without complaint and raised halls—beams aloft, eaves below—to roof him in, all so his reign might last.
entries.literal: Those who loved him desired his long endurance; they did not shrink from labor service; together they raised palaces with ridgepole above and rafters below to shelter him thickly, desiring his long endurance;

entries.zh: 敬之者欲其尊嚴，不憚勞煩，相與起作輿輪旌旗章表，以尊嚴之。
entries.en: Reverence made them wish him awe-inspiring rank, so they forged wheels, flew standards, and forged regalia that matched his majesty.
entries.literal: those who revered him desired his dignity; they did not shrink from toil and trouble; together they made chariot wheels, banners, flags, and insignia to lend him dignity.

entries.zh: 斯愛之至，敬之極也。
entries.en: Such was love pressed to its limit and reverence carried to its height.
entries.literal: This is the utmost of love and the extreme of reverence.

entries.zh: 苟心愛敬，雖報之至，情由未盡。
entries.en: Where love and reverence are genuine, no repayment, however lavish, can ever discharge the debt of feeling.
entries.literal: If in the heart there is true love and reverence, even when repayment reaches its utmost, the feeling still cannot be exhausted.

entries.zh: 或殺身以為之，盡其情也；
entries.en: Some laid down their lives—such was the depth of their devotion;
entries.literal: Some gave their bodies for it, exhausting their devotion;

entries.zh: 弈世以祀之，明其功也。
entries.en: generation after generation they kept his shrines lit, proclaiming his achievement to posterity.
entries.literal: age after age they sacrificed to him, clarifying his merit.

entries.zh: 是以流光與天地比長。
entries.en: Thus his fame runs on beside heaven and earth without end.
entries.literal: Therefore his flowing radiance vies in length with Heaven and Earth.

entries.zh: 後世聖人，知恤民之憂思深大者，必饗其樂；
entries.en: Later sages understood that rulers who take the people’s anxieties to heart are owed their joys in turn;
entries.literal: Later sages, knowing that those who deeply ponder the people’s cares must enjoy their pleasures;

entries.zh: 勤仁毓物使不夭折者，必受其福。
entries.en: and that those who labor at humanity, cherishing life so none dies before its time, earn a blessing in return.
entries.literal: those who labor at benevolence and nurture things so they do not die young must receive their blessing.

entries.zh: 故為之製禮以節之，使夫上仁繼天統物，不伐其功，民物安逸，若道自然，莫知所謝。
entries.en: So they framed rite and music to set bounds: the supreme humanity that carries heaven’s pattern and orders the world must never trumpet its own work; the people thrive as if by nature itself, unaware whom to praise.
entries.literal: Therefore they made ritual to regulate it, so that the highest benevolence, continuing Heaven’s thread and ordering things, did not boast of its achievement, and people and creatures rested at ease as if the way were spontaneous, none knowing whom to thank.

entries.zh: 《老子》曰：「聖人不仁，以百姓為芻狗」。
entries.en: Laozi writes: “The sage is not ‘kind’ in the small sense; he holds the common people as ritual straw dogs—deployed without clinging.”
entries.literal: The Laozi says: “The sage is not benevolent; he treats the hundred surnames like straw dogs.”

entries.zh: 此之謂也。
entries.en: The passage means just this.
entries.literal: This is what it refers to.

entries.zh: 上古穴居而野處，衣毛而冒皮，未有制度。
entries.en: In earliest times people lived in caves and the wilderness, wore pelts and raw hides, and had no fixed dress code at all.
entries.literal: In high antiquity people dwelt in caves and lived in the open; they clothed themselves in fur and covered their heads with hides, and there were yet no regulations.

entries.zh: 後世聖人易之以絲麻，觀翬翟之文，榮華之色，乃染帛以效之，始作五采，成以爲服。
entries.en: Later sages introduced silk and linen, took inspiration from the plumage of kingfishers and the sheen of costly furs, dyed cloth to match those colors, and so established the five-color system that became formal dress.
entries.literal: Later sages replaced these with silk and hemp; observing the patterns of kingfisher and sable and the splendor of their colors, they dyed fabrics to imitate them, first devised the five hues, and completed them as garments.

entries.zh: 見鳥獸有冠角髯胡之製，遂作冠冕纓蕤，以爲首飾。
entries.en: Noting how birds and beasts wore crests, horns, and beards by nature, tailors fashioned caps and crowns with hanging tassels as deliberate head ornaments.
entries.literal: Seeing that birds and beasts had crowns, horns, whiskers, and beards by nature, they then made caps, crowns, tassels, and drooping ornaments for headgear.

entries.zh: 凡十二章。
entries.en: The full set comprises twelve symbolic motifs.
entries.literal: In all there are twelve emblems.

entries.zh: 故《易》曰：「庖犧氏之王天下也，仰觀象於天，俯觀法於地，觀鳥獸之文，與地之宜，近取諸身，遠取諸物，於是始作八卦，以通神明之德，以類萬物之情。」
entries.en: The Book of Changes thus says of the sage-king Baoxi: "he read the sky and the earth, studied the markings of animals and the lay of the land, took lessons from his own body and from things around him, and from this devised the eight trigrams to link human ritual with spiritual power and to give order to the myriad phenomena."
entries.literal: Therefore the Changes says: “When Baoxi ruled the realm, he looked up to observe images in heaven, looked down to observe patterns on earth, observed the markings of birds and beasts and the suitability of the land, drew the near from his own person and the far from things, and thereby first created the eight trigrams, to communicate the virtue of spirits and gods and to classify the conditions of the myriad things.”

entries.zh: 黃帝、堯、舜垂衣裳而天下治，蓋取諸乾巛。
entries.en: The Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun are said to have “let robe and skirt fall straight,” and good government followed—an image drawn, tradition holds, from the trigrams Qian and Kun.
entries.literal: The Yellow Emperor, Yao, and Shun let their upper and lower garments hang down and the realm was well governed; this is thought to have been taken from Qian and Kun.

entries.zh: 乾巛有文，故上衣玄，下裳黃。
entries.en: Because Qian and Kun embody distinct patterns, ritual dress paired a black upper robe with a yellow lower skirt.
entries.literal: Qian and Kun have their patterns; therefore the upper garment is black and the lower skirt is yellow.

entries.zh: 日月星辰，山龍華蟲，作繢宗彝，藻火粉米，黼黻絺繡，以五采章施於五色作服。
entries.en: The twelve emblems—sun, moon, constellations, mountains, dragons, and the rest, down to the paired axe motifs—were woven in the five prescribed colors into the imperial vestments.
entries.literal: Sun, moon, and stars; mountains, dragons, and splendid insects; the ancestral urn as embroidery; water-weed, fire, powdered grain, and rice; axe-figures and opposing “fu” motifs in fine embroidery—the five colors were applied in five hues to make the robes.

entries.zh: 天子備章，公自山以下，侯伯自華蟲以下，子男自藻火以下，卿大夫自粉米以下。
entries.en: The emperor wore all twelve motifs; high nobility stepped down by rank—dukes kept the mountain and below, marquises the “splendid insect” and below, and so on until ministers were limited to the humbler symbols.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven had the full set of emblems; dukes from the mountains downward; marquises and earls from the splendid insect downward; viscounts and barons from water-weed and fire downward; ministers and grandees from powdered grain downward.

entries.zh: 至周而變之，以三辰爲旂旗。
entries.en: The Zhou revised the scheme, reserving sun, moon, and stars chiefly for flags rather than the robe itself.
entries.literal: By the Zhou they altered this, using the three luminaries for banners and flags.

entries.zh: 王祭上帝，則大裘而冕；
entries.en: For the supreme sacrifice to Heaven the king donned the heavy fur outer robe and the jeweled mianguan.
entries.literal: When the king sacrificed to High God, he wore the great fur robe and the mianguan;

entries.zh: 公侯卿大夫之服用九章以下。
entries.en: Nobles and senior officials were limited to nine emblems or fewer on their court dress.
entries.literal: The robes of dukes, marquises, and ministers and grandees used nine emblems or fewer.

entries.zh: 秦以戰國即天子位，滅去禮學，郊祀之服皆以袀玄。
entries.en: The Qin founders, rising from military conquest, discarded classical ritual; even suburban sacrifices were performed in undecorated black.
entries.literal: Qin, having taken the throne amid the Warring States, abolished ritual learning, and for suburban sacrifices the garments were all plain black.

entries.zh: 漢承秦故。
entries.en: The Han at first continued the austere Qin wardrobe.
entries.literal: Han inherited Qin practice.

entries.zh: 至世祖踐祚，都於土中，始修三雍，正兆七郊。
entries.en: Only when Guangwu took the throne and fixed his capital at Luoyang did the court revive the three ritual enclosures and set the seven directional suburban shrines in order.
entries.literal: When the Founding Emperor ascended the throne and made his capital in the central plain, he began to repair the three Yong ritual complexes and to align the seven suburban altars.

entries.zh: 顯宗遂就大業，初服旒冕，衣裳文章，赤舄絇屨，以祠天地，養三老五更於三雍，於時致治平矣。
entries.en: Emperor Ming finished what his father had begun: he appeared in full mianguan with hanging pearls, brocade upper and lower garments, and crimson ritual shoes, to worship Heaven and Earth and to host the aged worthies at the three Yong—by then the dress code matched the peace of the age.
entries.literal: The Manifest Emperor then completed the great enterprise: he first wore the flowing tassels and mianguan, patterned robe and skirt, red shoes with braided trim, to sacrifice to Heaven and Earth and to nurture the Three Elders and Five Exemplars in the three Yong; at that time good order was achieved.

entries.zh: 武冠，一曰武弁大冠，諸武官冠之。
entries.en: The great martial cap was the standard headgear of military officers.
entries.literal: The wuguan, one name is great martial bian; various military officials cap with it.

entries.zh: 侍中、中常侍加黃金璫，附蟬爲文，貂尾爲飾，謂之「趙惠文冠」。
entries.en: Palace attendants gilded the cap with a front cicada plaque and sable tail—hence the nickname “Marquis Huiwen crown.”
entries.literal: Palace attendants and regular palace attendants add a gold knob, cicada pattern in front, and sable tail as ornament; it is called the “Marquis Huiwen cap.”

entries.zh: 又名鵔鸃冠。
entries.en: It was also called the junyi cap.
entries.literal: It was also called the junyi cap.

entries.zh: 胡廣說曰：「趙武靈王效胡服，以金璫飾首，前插貂尾，爲貴職。
entries.en: Hu Guang explained: “King Wuling of Zhao copied Hu dress, using a gold knob to ornament the head, sable tails inserted in front, for exalted offices.
entries.literal: Hu Guang explained: “King Wuling of Zhao copied Hu dress, using a gold knob to ornament the head, sable tails inserted in front, for exalted offices.

entries.zh: 秦滅趙，以其君冠賜近臣。」
entries.en: After Qin swallowed Zhao, that princely cap passed to inner-court favorites."
entries.literal: When Qin destroyed Zhao, it gave the ruler’s cap to close attendants.”

entries.zh: 建武時，匈奴內屬，世祖賜南單於衣服，以中常侍惠文冠，中黃門童子佩刀云。
entries.en: When the Southern Chanyu came in during Jianwu, Guangwu presented him with court dress that included the golden cicada cap and yellow-gate boys with ritual swords.
entries.literal: In the Jianwu era, when the Xiongnu submitted, the Founding Emperor granted the Southern Chanyu clothing, with the attendant’s Huiwen cap and yellow-gate lads with girdle swords, it is said.

entries.zh: 安帝立皇太子，太子謁高祖廟、世祖廟，門大夫從，冠兩梁進賢；
entries.en: When Emperor An named a crown prince, the prince’s visits to the shrines of Gaozu and Guangwu were escorted by gate stewards in the two-ridged advance-the-worthy cap.
entries.literal: When Emperor An established the heir apparent, the heir visited the shrines to Gaozu and the Founding Emperor; gate grandees followed, capped with the two-ridge jinxianguan;

entries.zh: 洗馬冠高山。
entries.en: The heir apparent’s groom of the stable wore the high-mountain crown.
entries.literal: The groom of the heir apparent caps with the gaoshanguan.

entries.zh: 罷廟，侍御史任方奏請非乘從時，皆冠一梁，不宜以爲常服。
entries.en: After the imperial shrines closed, Censor Ren Fang urged that the single-ridged cap be reserved for processional duty and not treated as everyday wear.
entries.literal: When the temple visit ended, Attending Censor Ren Fang submitted a memorial asking that, except when riding in attendance, all should cap with one ridge, and that it was not suitable to take this as ordinary dress.

entries.zh: 事下有司。
entries.en: The throne referred the proposal to the ministries for review.
entries.literal: The matter was sent down to the responsible offices.

entries.zh: 尚書陳忠奏：「門大夫職如諫大夫，洗馬職如謁者，故皆服其服，先帝之舊也。
entries.en: Director Chen Zhong submitted: “The gate grandee’s duties are like those of a remonstrance grandee, and the groom’s are like those of an usher; therefore each wears that office’s dress—this was the former emperors’ old rule.
entries.literal: Director Chen Zhong submitted: “The gate grandee’s duties are like those of a remonstrance grandee, and the groom’s are like those of an usher; therefore each wears that office’s dress—this was the former emperors’ old rule.

entries.zh: 方言可寢。」
entries.en: Ren Fang’s words may be shelved.”
entries.literal: Ren Fang’s words may be shelved.”

entries.zh: 奏可。
entries.en: The emperor endorsed that view.
entries.literal: The memorial was approved.

entries.zh: 謁者，古者一名洗馬。
entries.en: The text adds that “usher” was once simply another term for groom.
entries.literal: The usher, in antiquity, had another name: groom of the stable.

entries.zh: 冕冠，垂旒，前後邃延，玉藻。
entries.en: The state crown was the mianguan—front and rear veils of pearls, with jade beads strung on the hanging threads.
entries.literal: The mianguan: hanging pearls, front and rear deep extensions, jade ornaments on the tassels.

entries.zh: 孝明皇帝永平二年，初詔有司採《周官》、《禮記》、《尚書·皋陶篇》，乘輿服從歐陽氏說，公卿以下從大小夏侯氏說。
entries.en: In 59 CE Emperor Ming directed the ministry to harmonize the Rites of Zhou, the Book of Rites, and the “Gao Yao” text: the emperor’s regalia followed the Ou-yang interpretation, while that of the bureaucracy followed the two Xiahou traditions.
entries.literal: In the second year of Yongping of Emperor Xiaoming, he first ordered the authorities to draw on the Offices of Zhou, the Record of Rites, and the “Gao Yao” chapter of the Documents: the imperial equipage followed the Ou-yang school, while dukes and ministers downward followed the Greater and Lesser Xiahou schools.

entries.zh: 冕皆廣七寸，長尺二寸，前圓後方，朱綠裏，玄上，前垂四寸，後垂三寸，系白玉珠爲十二旒，以其綬採色爲組纓。
entries.en: The standard mianguan measured seven inches by a foot two, round toward the audience and square at the back, lined in red-green and covered in black silk, with twelve white-jade strings of pearls whose tie-colors matched the wearer’s ribbon.
entries.literal: All mianguan are seven inches wide and one foot two inches long, round in front and square behind, with vermilion-green lining and black on top; the front hangs four inches and the rear three; white jade beads form twelve tassels, and the cord and tassel colors follow the ribbon’s hues.

entries.zh: 三公諸侯七旒，青玉爲珠；
entries.en: Dukes and enfeoffed lords were limited to seven pearl strings of green jade.
entries.literal: The Three Dukes and nobles have seven tassels, with green jade for beads;

entries.zh: 卿大夫五旒，黑玉爲珠。
entries.en: Senior ministers wore five strings, threaded with black jade.
entries.literal: ministers and grandees have five tassels, with black jade for beads.

entries.zh: 皆有前無後，各以其綬採色爲組纓，旁垂黈纊。
entries.en: These crowns had veils only in front; cords and tassels matched each man’s ribbon, with yellow silk wads at the temples.
entries.literal: All have front tassels but none behind; each uses his ribbon’s color for the cord and tassel, with yellow tassel-wads hanging at the side.

entries.zh: 郊天地，宗祀，明堂，則冠之。
entries.en: It was reserved for the greatest state sacrifices—to Heaven and Earth, the imperial ancestors, and inside the Bright Hall.
entries.literal: For suburban sacrifice to Heaven and Earth, for lineage sacrifice, and for the Bright Hall, they wear it.

entries.zh: 衣裳玉佩備章採，乘輿刺繡，公侯九卿以下皆織成，陳留襄邑獻之云。
entries.en: Court dress displayed the full set of emblems and jade girdle ornaments: the emperor’s was embroidered, while nobles and officials wore loom-woven brocade said to have been sent up each year from Xiangyi.
entries.literal: Robe and skirt, jade pendants, and full emblem colors are complete; the imperial equipage is embroidered, while dukes, marquises, and ministers downward all have woven fabric, presented, it is said, from Xiangyi in Chenliu.

entries.zh: 古者君臣佩玉，尊卑有度；
entries.en: Ancient courtiers all wore graded jade pendants to mark rank.
entries.literal: In antiquity lord and minister wore jade pendants, noble and base having their measures;

entries.zh: 上有韨，貴賤有殊。
entries.en: The leather kneepad above the sash likewise differed by station.
entries.literal: Above there was the fu kneepad, noble and base differing.

entries.zh: 佩，所以章德，服之衷也。
entries.en: Pendants advertised moral standing—the inward truth of the costume.
entries.literal: The pendant is that by which virtue is displayed; it is the inner of the dress.

entries.zh: 韍，所以執事，禮之共也。
entries.en: The kneepad marked readiness for ritual service—shared ceremonial equipment.
entries.literal: The fu is that by which one handles affairs; it is the shared ritual.

entries.zh: 故禮有其度，威儀之制，三代同之。
entries.en: Thus ornament and deportment stayed metered; the three dynasties held those rules in common.
entries.literal: Therefore ritual has its measures; the system of awesome bearing, the Three Dynasties share it.

entries.zh: 五霸迭興，戰兵不息，佩非戰器，韨非兵旗，於是解去韨佩，留其係璲，以爲章表。
entries.en: Endless warfare led hegemons to strip off heavy jade sets yet keep linked beads as badges of office.
entries.literal: The Five Hegemons rose in turn, war weapons did not cease; pendants were not battle gear, fu not battle banners; therefore they untied fu and pendants, kept their linked sui, and used them as insignia.

entries.zh: 故《詩》曰「鞙々佩璲」，此之謂也。
entries.en: The Odes’ “gleaming linked pendants” refer to this simplified regalia.
entries.literal: Therefore the Odes says “bright bright linked sui,” meaning this.

entries.zh: 韨佩既廢，秦乃以採組連結於璲，光明章表，轉相結受，故謂之綬。
entries.en: Qin replaced jade sets with bright silk cords knotted to seal-stones—origin of the named “ribbon” (shou).
entries.literal: Once fu and pendants were abolished, Qin used colored cords linked to the sui, bright and manifest as insignia, turning and receiving one another; therefore it is called the shou ribbon.

entries.zh: 漢承秦制，用而弗改，故加之以雙印佩刀之飾。
entries.en: Han kept Qin’s ribbons and layered on the double seal and court knife.
entries.literal: Han inherited Qin’s system, used it without change, and therefore added paired seals and girdle-knife ornament.

entries.zh: 至孝明皇帝，乃爲大佩，衝牙雙瑀璜，皆以白玉。
entries.en: Emperor Ming introduced the great court girdle—white jade pounding-teeth, paired disks, and huang plaques.
entries.literal: Down to Emperor Xiaoming he made the great pendant, pounding-fang, paired yu, and huang, all of white jade.

entries.zh: 乘輿落以白珠，公卿諸侯以採絲，其玉視冕旒，爲祭服云。
entries.en: The emperor’s set used pearl stringing; nobles used colored silk, with jade grades matching their crown tassels for sacrifice.
entries.literal: The imperial equipage threads them with white pearls; dukes and ministers use colored silk; the jade matches the mianguan tassels, for sacrificial dress, it is said.

entries.zh: 長冠，一曰齋冠，高七寸，廣三寸，促漆纚爲之，制如板，以竹爲裡。
entries.en: The “long cap,” also named the fasting cap, stood seven inches high, was stiffened with lacquered mesh over a bamboo frame, and looked like a narrow board on the head.
entries.literal: The changguan, also called the fasting cap, is seven inches high and three inches wide, made of tight-wrapped lacquered gauze, shaped like a board, with bamboo inside.

entries.zh: 初，高祖微時，以竹皮爲之，謂之劉氏冠，楚冠制也。
entries.en: When Liu Bang was still a commoner he fashioned such a cap from bamboo bark—the “Liu family cap,” modeled on southern Chu headgear.
entries.literal: At first, when Gaozu was still obscure, he made it from bamboo skin and called it the Liu clan cap, in the Chu cap style.

entries.zh: 民謂之鵲尾冠，非也。
entries.en: Folk nicknamed it the “magpie-tail cap,” but that name is a mistake.
entries.literal: The common people call it the magpie-tail cap; this is incorrect.

entries.zh: 祀宗廟諸祀則冠之。
entries.en: It was prescribed for ancestral rites and other major temple sacrifices.
entries.literal: For sacrifice in the ancestral temple and the various sacrifices they wear it.

entries.zh: 皆服袀玄，絳緣領袖爲中衣，絳褲襪，示其赤心奉神也。
entries.en: Wearers paired it with plain black robes, crimson-trimmed underlayers, and red legwear—symbolizing an undivided heart turned toward the gods.
entries.literal: All wear plain black, with crimson borders on collar and cuffs for the inner garment, crimson trousers and socks, showing their red hearts in serving the spirits.

entries.zh: 五郊，衣幘褲襪各如其色。
entries.en: At the five directional suburban altars, kerchief, leggings, and socks matched the color of the rite’s compass direction.
entries.literal: For the five suburban sacrifices, cap, kerchief, trousers, and socks each follow that quarter’s color.

entries.zh: 此冠高祖所造，故以爲祭服，尊敬之至也。
entries.en: Because the founder himself had devised it, the court treated this cap as the most solemn possible ritual headgear.
entries.literal: This cap was created by Gaozu, and therefore is taken as sacrificial dress, the utmost in reverence.

entries.zh: 進賢冠，古緇布冠也，文儒者之服也。
entries.en: The “advance-the-worthy” cap evolved from the ancient black cloth crown and identified scholars.
entries.literal: The jinxianguan is the ancient black cloth cap; it is the dress of literati.

entries.zh: 前高七寸，後高三寸，長八寸。
entries.en: It measured seven inches in front, three in back, and eight along the brim.
entries.literal: Seven inches high in front, three inches high in the rear, eight inches long.

entries.zh: 公侯三梁，中二千石以下至博士兩梁，自博士以下至小史私學弟子，皆一梁。
entries.en: The number of raised ribs signaled rank—three for the highest nobles, two for senior salary officials and academicians, one for everyone below.
entries.literal: Dukes and marquises have three ridges; from ministers at two thousand piculs down to erudits two ridges; from erudits downward to petty clerks and students of private schools, all have one ridge.

entries.zh: 宗室劉氏亦兩梁冠，示加服也。
entries.en: Even imperial kinsmen wore the two-ridged cap as a mark of honorific distinction.
entries.literal: Imperial clansmen of the Liu surname also wear the two-ridge cap, showing added dress.

entries.zh: 樊噲冠，漢將樊噲造次所冠，以入項羽軍。
entries.en: Fan Kuai’s famous rush into Xiang Yu’s camp gave this emergency military cap its name.
entries.literal: The Fan Kuai cap is what Han general Fan Kuai caps in haste to enter Xiang Yu’s camp.

entries.zh: 廣九寸，高七寸，前後出各四寸，制似冕。
entries.en: It was nine inches broad, seven tall, with four-inch brims front and back like a miniature state crown.
entries.literal: Nine inches wide, seven inches high, four inches protruding front and rear, patterned like a mianguan.

entries.zh: 司馬殿門大難，衛士服之。
entries.en: Guards donned it during the Sima Gate emergency.
entries.literal: At the great crisis at the Sima Gate, guards wear it.

entries.zh: 或曰，樊噲常持鐵楯，聞項羽有意殺漢王，噲裂裳以裹楯，冠之入軍門，立漢王旁，視項羽。
entries.en: Tradition adds that Fan Kuai wrapped his shield in a torn skirt, jammed on this cap, burst through the gate, and glared at Xiang Yu from Liu Bang’s side.
entries.literal: Some say Fan Kuai always held an iron shield; hearing that Xiang Yu intended to kill the King of Han, Kuai tore his skirt to wrap the shield, capped himself, entered the camp gate, and stood beside the King of Han, staring at Xiang Yu.

entries.zh: 冕冠 長冠 委貌冠 皮弁冠 爵弁冠 通天冠 遠湤冠 高山冠 進賢冠 法冠 武冠 建華冠 方山冠 巧士冠 卻非冠 卻敵冠 樊噲冠 術氏冠 鶡冠 幘 佩 刀 印 黃赤綬 赤綬 綠綬 紫綬 青綬 黑綬 黃綬 青紺綸 后夫人服
entries.en: This chapter treats the mianguan and other crown types, the ze, sword and seal regalia, the graded ribbons, and the dress of the empress and imperial consorts.
entries.literal: Mianguan (crown cap), changguan (long cap), weimaoguan (deferential-appearance cap), pibianguan (leather-skullcap), juebianguan (noble-skullcap), tongtianguan (pierce-heaven cap), yuanyouguan (far-roaming cap), gaoshanguan (high-mountain cap), jinxianguan (advance-the-worthy cap), faguan (law cap), wuguan (martial cap), jianhuaguan (splendid-bloom cap), fangshanguan (square-mountain cap), qiaoshiguan (ingenious-gentleman cap), quefeiguan (repel-wrong cap), quediguan (repel-enemy cap), Fan Kuai cap, Shi clan cap, heguan (pheasant cap), ze (kerchief), pei (pendants), dao (sword), yin (seal), yellow-red ribbon, red ribbon, green ribbon, purple ribbon, blue-green ribbon, black ribbon, yellow ribbon, blue-black twisted cord, and attire of the empress and consorts.

entries.zh: 衛紹王諱永濟，小字興勝，更諱允濟，章宗時避顯宗諱，詔改「允」為「永」。
entries.en: Wei Shaowang—taboo name Yongji, childhood name Xingsheng, once taboo-named Yunji—during Zhangzong's reign, because of the taboo on Xianzong's name, received an edict changing "Yun" to "Yong."
entries.literal: Wei Shaowang, taboo name Yongji, childhood name Xingsheng, formerly taboo-named Yunji; during Zhangzong's reign, to avoid Xianzong's taboo, an edict changed "Yun" to "Yong."

entries.zh: 世宗第七子，母曰元妃李氏。
entries.en: He was Shizong's seventh son; his mother was Yuan Consort Li.
entries.literal: He was the seventh son of Shizong; his mother was Yuan Consort of the Li clan.

entries.zh: 衛王長身，美髯鬚，天資儉約，不好華飾，大定十一年，封薛王。
entries.en: Prince Wei stood tall, with a fine beard; he was frugal by nature and shunned ornament. In Dading year 11 he was made Prince of Xue.
entries.literal: Prince Wei was tall, with a handsome beard; by nature he was frugal and disliked lavish adornment. In the eleventh year of Dading he was enfeoffed Prince of Xue.

entries.zh: 是歲，進封禭王。
entries.en: That year he was advanced to Prince of Cui.
entries.literal: That same year he was advanced to Prince of Cui.

entries.zh: 十七年，授世襲猛安。
entries.en: In year 17 he received a hereditary meng'an commission.
entries.literal: In the seventeenth year he was granted a hereditary meng'an.

entries.zh: 二十五年，加開府義同三司。
entries.en: In year 25 he was made grand marshal with ceremonial parity to the Three Excellencies.
entries.literal: In the twenty-fifth year he was given Grand Marshal with ceremonial parity to the Three Excellencies.

entries.zh: 二十六年，為秘書監。
entries.en: In year 26 he became director of the Secretariat.
entries.literal: In the twenty-sixth year he became Director of the Secretariat.

entries.zh: 明年，轉刑部尚書。
entries.en: The next year he was made minister of justice.
entries.literal: The next year he was transferred to Minister of Justice.

entries.zh: 又明年，改殿前都點檢。
entries.en: The year after that he became chief inspector of the palatial guards.
entries.literal: The year after, he was made Chief Inspector of the Palatial Guards.

entries.zh: 二十九年，世宗崩，章宗即位，進封潞王。
entries.en: In year 29 Shizong died and Zhangzong took the throne; he was advanced to Prince of Lu.
entries.literal: In the twenty-ninth year Shizong died and Zhangzong ascended; he was advanced to Prince of Lu.

entries.zh: 起複，判安武軍節度使。
entries.en: He left mourning and was posted as military governor of Anwu Army.
entries.literal: He left mourning and was assigned as military governor of Anwu Army.

entries.zh: 五月，至冀州，以到任表謝，賜詔優答。
entries.en: In the fifth month he reached Jizhou, thanked the throne for his appointment, and received a warm reply edict.
entries.literal: In the fifth month he reached Jizhou, submitted a memorial of thanks on taking office, and received a gracious reply edict.

entries.zh: 明昌二年，進封韓王。
entries.en: In Mingchang year 2 he was advanced to Prince of Han.
entries.literal: In the second year of Mingchang he was advanced to Prince of Han.

entries.zh: 四年，改判興平軍。
entries.en: In year 4 he was reassigned to Xingping Army.
entries.literal: In the fourth year he was reassigned to Xingping Army.

entries.zh: 五年，改沁南軍。
entries.en: In year 5 he was transferred to Qinnan Army.
entries.literal: In the fifth year he was transferred to Qinnan Army.

entries.zh: 承安二年，改封衛王。
entries.en: In Chengan year 2 he was made Prince of Wei.
entries.literal: In the second year of Chengan he was made Prince of Wei.

entries.zh: 三年，改昭義軍。
entries.en: In year 3 he was assigned to Zhaoyi Army.
entries.literal: In the third year he was assigned to Zhaoyi Army.

entries.zh: 泰和元年，改判彰德府事。
entries.en: In the first year of Taihe he was put in charge of Zhangde Prefecture.
entries.literal: In the first year of Taihe he was put in charge of Zhangde Prefecture.

entries.zh: 五年，改判平陽府。
entries.en: In year 5 he was put in charge of Pingyang Prefecture.
entries.literal: In the fifth year he was put in charge of Pingyang Prefecture.

entries.zh: 初，章宗誅鄭王永蹈、趙王永中，久，頗悔之。
entries.en: At first Zhangzong had put Prince of Zheng Yongtao and Prince of Zhao Yongzhong to death; in time he came to regret it deeply.
entries.literal: Initially Zhangzong had executed Prince of Zheng Yongtao and Prince of Zhao Yongzhong; after a long while he deeply regretted it.

entries.zh: 七年，下詔追復舊封，仍賜諡。
entries.en: In year 7 he issued an edict restoring their former titles and bestowing posthumous names.
entries.literal: In the seventh year he issued an edict posthumously restoring their former titles and granting posthumous names.

entries.zh: 而永蹈無後，乃以衛王子按陳為鄭王後，賜衛王詔曰：「朕念鄭王自棄天常，以幹國憲，槁瘞曠野，忽諸不祀。
entries.en: Yongtao left no heir, so Prince Wei's son An Chen was made heir to Prince of Zheng. The edict to Prince Wei ran: "I think of Prince of Zheng, who threw away Heaven's law and breached the state's statutes, left to wither in the wild, and passed from sacrifice altogether.
entries.literal: Yongtao had no heir, so the Prince of Wei's son An Chen was made successor to Prince of Zheng. An edict to Prince Wei said: "I reflect on Prince of Zheng, who abandoned Heaven's constants and violated state law, withered in burial on the open plain, gone suddenly without sacrifice.

entries.zh: 歷歲既久，深用愴然。
entries.en: Years have gone by, and grief weighs on me.
entries.literal: Years have passed and I am deeply grieved.

entries.zh: 親親之情。
entries.en: Kinship tugs at the heart.
entries.literal: The bonds of kin weigh upon me.

entries.zh: 有懷難置。
entries.en: I cannot set the feeling aside.
entries.literal: My heart cannot find rest.

entries.zh: 已詔追復舊爵，改葬如儀。
entries.en: I have already ordered his old rank restored and a proper reburial.
entries.literal: I have already ordered his former title restored and burial redone according to rite.

entries.zh: 稽考古禮，以卿之子按陳為鄭王後，謹其祭祀，卿其悉之。」
entries.en: By the ancient rites, your son An Chen is made heir to Prince of Zheng to keep his sacrifices—take full heed of this."
entries.literal: Examining ancient rites, I make your son An Chen successor to Prince of Zheng to tend his sacrifices—see that you know this fully."

entries.zh: 已而改武定軍節度使。
entries.en: Thereafter he was posted as military governor of Wuding Army.
entries.literal: Thereafter he was reassigned as military governor of Wuding Army.

entries.zh: 八年十一月，自武定軍入朝。
entries.en: In the eleventh month of year 8 he came to court from Wuding Army.
entries.literal: In the eleventh month of the eighth year he entered court from Wuding Army.

entries.zh: 是時，章宗已感嗽疾，衛王且辭行，而章宗意留之。
entries.en: By then Zhangzong had fallen ill with a cough; Prince Wei was ready to depart, but Zhangzong meant to keep him at court.
entries.literal: By then Zhangzong had contracted a coughing illness; Prince Wei was about to take leave, but Zhangzong intended to keep him.

entries.zh: 宗章初年，雅愛諸王，置王傳府尉官以傳導德義。
entries.en: Early in Zhangzong's reign he had loved his brothers dearly and set tutors and household officers in each prince's house to teach virtue.
entries.literal: At the beginning of Zhangzong's reign he had dearly loved the princes and appointed tutors and household officers in each princely establishment to convey moral teaching.

entries.zh: 及永中、永蹈之誅，由是疏忌宗室，遂以王傅府尉檢制王家，苛部嚴密，門戶出入皆有籍。
entries.en: After Yongzhong and Yongtao were killed, he grew wary of the clan and turned the princes' tutors and household officers into overseers—rules were tight, and every coming and going at the gates was logged.
entries.literal: After the executions of Yongzhong and Yongtao, he grew distant and suspicious of the imperial clan, and used princes' tutors and household officers to control princely households—harshly regulated, with every entry and exit recorded.

entries.zh: 而衛王乃永蹈母弟，柔弱鮮智能，故章宗愛之。
entries.en: Prince Wei was Yongtao's uterine younger brother—soft, ungifted, and mild—so Zhangzong held him dear.
entries.literal: Prince Wei was Yongtao's younger brother by the same mother—gentle, weak, and little gifted—so Zhangzong favored him.

entries.zh: 既無繼嗣，而諸叔兄弟多在，章宗皆不肯立，惟欲立衛王，故於辭行留之。
entries.en: He had no son, and many uncles and brothers still lived; Zhangzong would raise none of them, wishing only to make Prince Wei heir—so when Prince Wei tried to leave, he was kept back.
entries.literal: With no heir of his own and many uncles and brothers still living, Zhangzong would establish none of them; he only wished to make Prince Wei his successor, and therefore detained him when he sought to leave.

entries.zh: 無何，章宗大漸，元妃李氏、黃門李新喜、平章政事完顏匡定策。
entries.en: Soon Zhangzong was near death; Yuan Consort Li, palace attendant Li Xinxhi, and Grand Councilor Wanyan Kuang fixed the succession.
entries.literal: Before long Zhangzong fell critically ill; Yuan Consort Li, Palace Attendant Li Xinxhi, and Grand Councilor Wanyan Kuang settled the plan.

entries.zh: 章宗崩，匡等傳遣詔，立衛王。
entries.en: Zhangzong died; Kuang and his party passed on the final edict and set Prince Wei on the throne.
entries.literal: Zhangzong died; Kuang and the others transmitted the death edict and enthroned Prince Wei.

entries.zh: 衛王固讓，乃承詔舉哀，即皇帝位於柩前。
entries.en: Prince Wei refused at first, then took the edict, raised the lament, and became emperor before the bier.
entries.literal: Prince Wei firmly declined, then accepted the edict and mourned, ascending the throne before the coffin.

entries.zh: 明日，群臣朝見于大安殿。
entries.en: Next day the hundred officials attended him in the Hall of Great Peace.
entries.literal: The next day the hundred officials paid homage in the Hall of Great Peace.

entries.zh: 詔路府州縣為大行皇帝服七日。
entries.en: An edict ordered every circuit, prefecture, and county to mourn the late emperor for seven days.
entries.literal: An edict ordered circuit, prefecture, and county offices to observe seven days' mourning for the late emperor.

entries.zh: 天會五年，宗望薨，帝為右副元帥，駐兵燕京。
entries.en: In the fifth year of Tianhui Zongwang died; the emperor became right deputy commander-in-chief and stationed troops at Yanjing.
entries.literal: In the fifth year of Tianhui Zongwang died; the emperor became right deputy commander-in-chief and stationed troops at Yanjing.

entries.zh: 十一月，分遣諸將伐宋，帝發自河間，徇地淄、青。
entries.en: In the eleventh month the generals were divided and sent against Song; the emperor set out from Hejian and pacified Zi and Qing.
entries.literal: In the eleventh month the generals were divided and sent against Song; the emperor set out from Hejian and pacified Zi and Qing.

entries.zh: 六年正月，宋馬括兵二十萬至樂安，帝率師擊破之。
entries.en: In the first month of the sixth year Song general Ma Kuo with two hundred thousand troops reached Le'an; the emperor led his army and defeated them.
entries.literal: In the first month of the sixth year Song general Ma Kuo with two hundred thousand troops reached Le'an; the emperor led his army and defeated them.

entries.zh: 聞宋主在揚州，時東作方興，留大軍夾河屯田而還，軍山西。
entries.en: Hearing the Song ruler was at Yangzhou and that spring planting was underway, he left the main army to farm both banks of the river and withdrew, encamping in Shanxi.
entries.literal: Hearing the Song ruler was at Yangzhou and that spring planting was underway, he left the main army to farm both banks of the river and withdrew, encamping in Shanxi.

entries.zh: 二月，移剌古破宋台宗雋、宋忠軍五萬於大名，明日再破之，獲宗雋、忠而還。
entries.en: In the second month Yelü Gu broke fifty thousand troops of Song generals Tai Zongjun and Song Zhong at Daming; the next day he defeated them again, captured Zongjun and Zhong, and returned.
entries.literal: In the second month Yelü Gu broke fifty thousand troops of Song generals Tai Zongjun and Song Zhong at Daming; the next day he defeated them again, captured Zongjun and Zhong, and returned.

entries.zh: 冀州人乘夜出兵襲照裏營。
entries.en: People of Jizhou by night sent troops to raid Zhaoli's camp.
entries.literal: People of Jizhou by night sent troops to raid Zhaoli's camp.

entries.zh: 照裏擊敗之。
entries.en: Zhaoli defeated them.
entries.literal: Zhaoli defeated them.

entries.zh: 宋主奉表請和，密書以誘契丹、漢人。
entries.en: The Song ruler submitted a memorial begging peace and sent secret letters to entice the Khitan and Han.
entries.literal: The Song ruler submitted a memorial begging peace and sent secret letters to entice the Khitan and Han.

entries.zh: 詔伐宋。
entries.en: An edict ordered war on Song.
entries.literal: An edict ordered war on Song.

entries.zh: 帝發自河北，降滑州，取開德府，攻大名府，克之，河北平。
entries.en: The emperor set out from Hebei, reduced Huazhou, took Kaide Prefecture, attacked Daming Prefecture, captured it, and Hebei was pacified.
entries.literal: The emperor set out from Hebei, reduced Huazhou, took Kaide Prefecture, attacked Daming Prefecture, captured it, and Hebei was pacified.

entries.zh: 景宣帝
entries.en: Emperor Jingxuan.
entries.literal: Emperor Jingxuan.

entries.zh: 金有天下百餘年，曆惟一易。
entries.en: Jin held the realm for a little over a century and changed its calendar only once.
entries.literal: Jin held the realm for a hundred-odd years, and the calendar changed only once.

entries.zh: 天會五年，司天楊級紹造《大明曆》，十五年春正月朔，始頒行之。
entries.en: In Tianhui year 5 the Director of Heaven Yang Ji completed the Grand Clarity Calendar; in spring of year 15, on the new moon of the first month, it was first promulgated.
entries.literal: In the fifth year of Tianhui, the Director of Heaven Yang Ji succeeded in making the "Grand Clarity Calendar"; in spring of the fifteenth year, first month new moon, it was first promulgated.

entries.zh: 其法，以三億八千三百七十六萬八千六百五十七為曆元，五千二百三十為日法。
entries.en: Its constants take 383,768,657 as the calendar origin and 5,230 as the day divisor.
entries.literal: Its method: 383,768,657 as calendar origin; 5,230 as day divisor.

entries.zh: 然其所本，不能詳究，或曰因宋《紀元曆》而增損之也。
entries.en: Its sources cannot be traced in full; some say it was adapted from the Song Era Origin Calendar with additions and cuts.
entries.literal: Yet its foundation cannot be traced in detail—or so it is said, it was augmented and reduced from the Song "Era Origin Calendar."

entries.zh: 正隆戊寅三月辛酉朔，司天言日當食，而不食。
entries.en: Zhenglong, wuyin year, third month, on xinyou, the new moon: the calendar office predicted an eclipse, but none occurred.
entries.literal: Zhenglong, year wuyin, third month, on xinyou the new moon: the Director of Heaven said the sun should eclipse, but it did not.

entries.zh: 大定癸巳五月壬辰朔，日食，甲午十一月甲申朔，日食，加時皆先天。
entries.en: Dading guisi, fifth month, on renchen, the new moon—a solar eclipse; jiawu, eleventh month, on jiashen, the new moon—another eclipse; in both cases the predicted time came before the event.
entries.literal: Dading guisi, fifth month on renchen the new moon—solar eclipse; jiawu, eleventh month on jiashen the new moon—solar eclipse; in each case the predicted hour came before the event.

entries.zh: 丁酉九月丁酉朔，食乃後天。
entries.en: Dingyou, ninth month, on dingyou, the new moon—the eclipse came after the predicted hour.
entries.literal: Dingyou, ninth month, on dingyou the new moon—the eclipse came after the predicted hour.

entries.zh: 由是占候漸差，乃命司天監趙知微重修《大明曆》，十一年曆成。
entries.en: Prognostication and observation drifted apart; Zhao Zhiwei, Director of the Astronomical Directorate, was therefore ordered to revise the Grand Clarity Calendar, and in the eleventh year the calendar was completed.
entries.literal: From this prognostication and observation drifted; therefore Zhao Zhiwei, Director of the Astronomical Directorate, was ordered to revise the Grand Clarity Calendar—it was completed in the eleventh year.

entries.zh: 時翰林應奉耶律履亦造《乙未曆》。
entries.en: At the same time Hanlin Attendant Yelü Lü also devised the Yiwei Calendar.
entries.literal: At that time Hanlin Attendant Yelü Lü also devised the "Yiwei Calendar."

entries.zh: 二十一年十一月望，太陰虧食，遂命尚書省委禮部員外郎任忠傑與司天曆官驗所食時刻分秒，比校知微、履及見行曆之親疏，以知微曆為親，遂用之。
entries.en: In year 21, at the full moon of the eleventh month, the moon was eclipsed; the Ministry ordered Ren Zhongjie of the Rites Bureau and the calendar officers to verify the hour, minute, and second of the eclipse and compare Zhao Zhiwei's, Yelü Lü's, and the current calendar—Zhiwei's proved closer, and his calendar was adopted.
entries.literal: Twenty-first year, eleventh month full moon, the moon suffered eclipse; therefore ordered Ministry of Rites Vice Director Ren Zhongjie with calendar officers to verify the hour, minute, and second of the eclipse, compare the closeness of Zhiwei's, Lü's, and the current calendars—Zhiwei's was closer, and it was adopted.

entries.zh: 明昌初，司天又改進新曆，禮部郎中張行簡言：「請俟他日月食，覆校無差，然後用之。」
entries.en: Early in Mingchang the calendar office proposed yet another revision; Zhang Xingjian, Director of the Ministry of Rites, said, "Please wait for another solar or lunar eclipse, re-check until there is no discrepancy, and only then adopt it."
entries.literal: Early Mingchang, the Directorate again reformed a new calendar; Zhang Xingjian, Director of Rites, said: "Please wait for another solar or lunar eclipse, re-verify without discrepancy, then use it."

entries.zh: 事遂寢。
entries.en: The proposal was shelved.
entries.literal: The matter was then shelved.

entries.zh: 是以終金之世，惟用知微曆，我朝初亦用之，後始改《授時曆》焉。
entries.en: Through the whole Jin age only Zhao Zhiwei's calendar was used; our dynasty used it at first as well, then replaced it with the Season-Granting Calendar.
entries.literal: Thus through Jin's age only Zhiwei's calendar was used; our dynasty at first used it too, then changed to the Season-Granting Calendar.

entries.zh: 今其書存乎太史，采而錄之，以為《曆志》。
entries.en: Its text still rests with the Grand Astrologer; we have gathered and recorded it here as the Calendar Treatise.
entries.literal: Now its text remains with the Grand Astrologer; we gather and record it as the Calendar Treatise.

entries.zh: 昔者聖人因天道以授人時，厘百工以熙庶政，步推之法，其來尚矣。
entries.en: Long ago the sages took Heaven's Way to give mankind the seasons, set the hundred offices in order to brighten common affairs—and the arts of stepwise reckoning reach back to a remote antiquity.
entries.literal: In antiquity the sages, taking Heaven's Way to grant mankind the seasons, ordered the hundred offices to brighten the multitude of government affairs—the methods of stepwise reckoning, their origin is remote indeed.

entries.zh: 自漢太初迄于前宋，治曆者奚啻七十餘家，大概或百年或數十年，率一易焉。
entries.en: From the Han Taichu era down to the former Song, calendar-makers numbered more than seventy houses; as a rule, every century or few decades brought a new system.
entries.literal: From Han Taichu down to the former Song, calendar-makers were no fewer than seventy-odd houses; broadly, whether a century or several decades, on average there was one change.

entries.zh: 蓋日月五星盈縮進退，與夫天運，至不齊也，人方制器以求之，以俾其齊，積寡至多，不能無爽故爾。
entries.en: Sun, moon, and five stars swell and shrink, advance and retreat; Heaven's motion is never uniform. Men fashion reckonings to force alignment—but piling small errors into large ones, some discrepancy is inevitable.
entries.literal: For sun, moon, and five stars have expansion, contraction, advance and retreat, and Heaven's motion is utterly uneven—men then fashion instruments to seek alignment, to make it even; but accumulating few into many, error cannot be avoided.

entries.zh: 五行之精氣，在天為五緯，在地為五材，在人為五常及五事。
entries.en: The refined qi of the Five Elements becomes the five planets in Heaven, the five materials on Earth, and in humanity the Five Constants and the Five Affairs.
entries.literal: The quintessential qi of the Five Elements—in Heaven are the five planets, on Earth the five materials, in humanity the Five Constants and the Five Affairs.

entries.zh: 五緯志諸《天文》，歷代皆然。
entries.en: The five planets are recorded in the Astronomy treatises, as every dynasty has done.
entries.literal: Records of the five planets belong in the Astronomy treatises, as in every dynasty.

entries.zh: 其形質在地，性情在人，休咎各以其類，為感應於兩間者，歷代又有《五行志》焉。
entries.en: Form and substance belong to Earth, disposition to humanity; auspicious and inauspicious signs each keep to their kind—as resonances between the two realms—and dynasties have also compiled Treatises on the Five Elements.
entries.literal: Their form and substance lie on Earth, their disposition in humanity; auspicious and inauspicious signs each follow their kind—as responses between the two realms—dynasties have also compiled Treatises on the Five Elements.

entries.zh: 兩漢以來，儒者若夏侯勝之徒，專以《洪範五行》為學，作史者多采其說，凡言某征之休咎，則以某事之得失系之，而配之以五行。
entries.en: Since the Two Han, scholars such as Xiahou Sheng took the Hong Fan's Five Elements as their whole craft; historians mostly followed them—whenever they judged an omen auspicious or inauspicious, they bound it to some affair's success or failure and paired it with the Five Elements.
entries.literal: Since the Two Han, scholars such as Xia Hou Sheng made the Hong Fan's Five Elements their sole study; historians mostly adopted their views—whenever they spoke of the auspicious or inauspicious bearing of some omen, they tied it to the success or failure of some affair and matched it to the Five Elements.

entries.zh: 謂其盡然，其弊不免于傅會；
entries.en: To hold this wholly true cannot escape the fault of forced correlation;
entries.literal: To hold this wholly true cannot escape the fault of forced correlation;

entries.zh: 謂其不然，「肅，時雨若」、「蒙，恆風若」之類，箕子蓋嘗言之。
entries.en: to hold it wholly false—sayings such as "With respect, seasonable rain follows" and "With obscurity, constant wind follows"—Jizi surely spoke them.
entries.literal: to hold it wholly false—sayings such as "With respect, seasonable rain follows" and "With obscurity, constant wind follows"—Jizi surely spoke them.

entries.zh: 金世未能一天下，天文災祥猶有星野之說，五行休咎見於國內者不得他諉，乃匯其史氏所書，仍前史法，作《五行志》。
entries.en: The Jin age had not united the realm; celestial disaster and blessing still invoked the doctrine of stellar fields, yet Five Elements omens seen within their borders could not be blamed on others—so they gathered what their historians recorded, following earlier annalistic form, and composed this Treatise on the Five Elements.
entries.literal: The Jin age could not unite all under Heaven; celestial disaster and blessing still spoke of astrological fields, but Five Elements omens appearing within the realm could not be blamed elsewhere—so they gathered what their historians wrote, following earlier annalistic form, and composed this Treatise on the Five Elements.

entries.zh: 至於五常五事之感應，則不必泥漢儒為例雲。
entries.en: As for responses of the Five Constants and Five Affairs, there is no need to bind oneself to Han Confucian precedent.
entries.literal: As for responses of the Five Constants and Five Affairs, there is no need to bind oneself to Han Confucian precedent.

entries.zh: 十四年八月庚戌，文武百僚、太師宗磐等上議曰：「國家肇造區夏，四征弗庭，太祖武元皇帝受命撥亂，光啟大業。
entries.en: On the gengxu day of the eighth month of year 14, the civil and military officials, led by Grand Preceptor Zong Pan, memorialized: 'From the founding of the realm within the Central Lands, with expeditions on every side bringing distant lords to court, Emperor Taizu, the Martial Primary Emperor, took Heaven's mandate to quell chaos and brilliantly opened the great enterprise.
entries.literal: On the gengxu day of the eighth month of the fourteenth year, the civil and military officials, Grand Preceptor Zong Pan, and others submitted a memorial stating: 'Since the state was first established within the Central Realm and campaigns on all four sides brought the recalcitrant to court, Emperor Taizu, the Martial Primary Emperor, received Heaven's mandate to quell disorder and brilliantly inaugurated the great enterprise.

entries.zh: 太宗文烈皇帝繼志卒伐，奮張惶威。
entries.en: Emperor Taizong, the Wenlie Emperor, carried on that purpose to its end and spread a majesty that made the realm tremble.
entries.literal: Emperor Taizong, the Wenlie Emperor, carried forward his aim and completed his conquests, extending awe-inspiring might.

entries.zh: 原其積德累功，所由來者遠矣！
entries.en: When one traces the virtue and merit accumulated over generations, their roots lie deep in the distant past!
entries.literal: Tracing the accumulation of virtue and merit through generations, their origins lie far in the past!

entries.zh: 且禮多為貴，固前籍之美談；
entries.en: Moreover, ritual holds that to multiply honors is the highest esteem—a celebrated maxim of the ancient books;
entries.literal: Moreover, in ritual to multiply honors is esteemed—a fine saying of former records;

entries.zh: 德厚流光，實本朝之先務。
entries.en: When virtue runs deep its light reaches later ages—this is truly a foremost duty of our house.
entries.literal: Deep virtue shines upon posterity—this is truly a foremost duty of our dynasty.

entries.zh: 伏惟皇九代祖，廓君人之量，挺禦世之姿。
entries.en: We humbly reflect that the imperial ancestor nine generations back possessed the breadth of a true sovereign and the bearing to master an age.
entries.literal: Humbly considering the ninth-generation imperial ancestor, he possessed the measure of a ruler of men and bore the stature to govern the age.

entries.zh: 虞舜生馮，遷于負夏，太王避狄，邑此岐山，聖姥來歸，天原肇發。
entries.en: As when Shun was born at Feng and moved to Fuxia, or when King Tai fled the Di and settled at Mount Qi—when the Holy Matriarch came into the clan, the heavenly origin of the house first unfolded.
entries.literal: When Yu Shun was born at Feng and moved to Fuxia, when King Tai fled the Di and made his seat at Mount Qi—when the Holy Matriarch came to join the clan, the heavenly origin first unfolded.

entries.zh: 皇八代祖、皇七代祖，承家襲慶，裕後垂芳，不求赫赫之名，終大振振之族。
entries.en: The imperial ancestors of the eighth and seventh generations inherited the family fortune and spread blessing to their descendants; though they sought no dazzling renown, in the end they greatly strengthened the clan.
entries.literal: The eighth- and seventh-generation imperial ancestors inherited the family fortune and extended blessings to posterity; though they sought no illustrious fame, in the end they greatly invigorated the clan.

entries.zh: 皇六代祖，徒居得吉，播種是勤，去暴露獲棟宇之安，釋負載興車輿之利。
entries.en: The sixth-generation imperial ancestor moved to an auspicious place and was tireless in sowing; he left life in the open for the security of roofed halls, set down his burdens, and brought the people the benefit of carts and carriages.
entries.literal: The sixth-generation imperial ancestor, moving to an auspicious site, was diligent in sowing seed; he left exposure to the elements and gained the security of roofed dwellings, laid down burdens and brought forth the benefit of carts.

entries.zh: 皇五代祖孛堇，雄姿邁世，美略齊時。
entries.en: The fifth-generation imperial ancestor Boqin had a heroic bearing that outstripped his age and a grand strategy equal to his times.
entries.literal: The fifth-generation imperial ancestor Boqin had a heroic presence that surpassed his age and grand designs that matched his times.

entries.zh: 成百里日辟之功，戎車既飾；
entries.en: He accomplished the feat of opening a hundred li in a single day, and the war chariots were already fitted for battle;
entries.literal: He achieved the work of opening a hundred li in a day, and the war chariots were already adorned;

entries.zh: 著五教在寬之訓，人紀肇修。
entries.en: He set forth the teaching of the Five Doctrines with leniency at their core, and human relations were first brought into order.
entries.literal: He established the instruction of the Five Teachings through leniency, and human relations were first put in order.

entries.zh: 皇高祖太師，質自天成，德為民望，兼精騎射，往無不摧，始置官師，歸者益眾。
entries.en: The imperial great-great-grandfather, Grand Preceptor, was plain and honest by nature and a moral beacon for the people; expert in mounted archery, he went forth and nothing stood before him; when he first appointed officials and teachers, ever more tribes came to submit.
entries.literal: The imperial great-grandfather, Grand Preceptor, was by nature plain and honest, a moral paragon for the people; skilled alike in mounted archery, he went forth and nothing could withstand him; when he first established officials and teachers, those who came to submit grew ever more numerous.

entries.zh: 皇曾祖太師，威靈震遠，機警絕人，雅善運籌，未嘗衿甲，臨敵愈奮，應變若神。
entries.en: The imperial great-grandfather, Grand Preceptor, whose authority and majesty shook distant lands and whose alertness surpassed all others, excelled in strategy and never took the field lightly clad in armor; facing the enemy he fought all the harder, adapting to change like a spirit.
entries.literal: The imperial great-great-grandfather, Grand Preceptor, his authority and majesty shook distant lands, his alertness surpassed other men; he excelled in stratagem and never donned armor lightly; facing the enemy he grew only fiercer, responding to change like a spirit.

entries.zh: 皇曾叔祖太師，機獨運心，公無私物，四方聳動，諸部歸懷，德威兩隆，風俗大定。
entries.en: The imperial great-granduncle, Grand Preceptor, whose designs sprang from the heart alone and whose public service knew no private gain, stirred the four quarters until every tribe returned in allegiance; virtue and awe alike rose high, and customs were greatly settled.
entries.literal: The imperial great-great-granduncle, Grand Preceptor, his machinations proceeded from the heart alone, his public-mindedness admitted no private interest; the four quarters were stirred and all tribes returned in allegiance; virtue and awe alike rose high, and customs were greatly settled.

entries.zh: 皇伯祖太師，友于盡愛，國爾惟忠，謀必罔愆，舉無不濟。
entries.en: The imperial granduncle, Grand Preceptor, fulfilled all fraternal duty as a brother and harbored only loyalty toward the state; every plan was without flaw, and nothing he undertook failed.
entries.literal: The imperial granduncle, Grand Preceptor, as a brother fulfilled all fraternal love and toward the state harbored only loyalty; every plan was without error, and nothing he undertook failed.

entries.zh: 累代祖妣，婦道警戒，王業艱難，俱殫內助之勞，實著始基之漸。
entries.en: Consorts of successive generations observed wifely conduct with strict vigilance through the hardships of founding the royal enterprise; all exhausted themselves in support within the household and manifestly showed how the foundation was slowly laid.
entries.literal: Successive generations of imperial consorts observed wifely conduct with strict vigilance amid the hardships of building the royal enterprise; all exhausted themselves in inward support and manifestly showed the gradual laying of the foundation.

entries.zh: 是宜采群臣之僉議，酌故事以遵行，款帝於郊，稱天以誄。
entries.en: It is fitting to adopt the unanimous counsel of the officials, consult precedent and follow it, address Heaven at the suburban altar, and proclaim Heaven's praise in the eulogy.
entries.literal: It is fitting to adopt the unanimous counsel of the officials, consult precedent and carry it out, address Heaven at the suburban altar, and proclaim to Heaven in the eulogy.

entries.zh: 謹按諡法，布義行剛曰'景'，主義行德曰'元'，保民耆艾曰'明'，溫柔聖善曰'懿'，請上皇九代祖尊諡曰景元皇帝，廟號始祖，妣曰明懿皇后。
entries.en: According to the law of posthumous titles: 'jing' for spreading righteousness and acting with firmness, 'yuan' for upholding righteousness and practicing virtue, 'ming' for protecting the people and honoring the aged, 'yi' for gentle warmth and sagely goodness—we ask that the ninth-generation imperial ancestor receive the posthumous title Emperor Jingyuan, with the temple name Shizu, and that his consort be titled Empress Mingyi.
entries.literal: According to the Posthumous Title Law: 'jing' for spreading righteousness and acting with firmness, 'yuan' for upholding righteousness and practicing virtue, 'ming' for cherishing the aged who cherish the people, 'yi' for gentle warmth and sagely goodness—we request the posthumous honorific title Emperor Jingyuan for the ninth-generation imperial ancestor, with the temple name Shizu, and Empress Mingyi for his consort.

entries.zh: 中和純備曰'德'，道德純一曰'思'，請上皇八代祖尊諡曰德皇帝，妣曰思皇后。
entries.en: De is for perfect centrality and harmony, si for pure unity of virtue and the Way—we ask that the eighth-generation imperial ancestor receive the posthumous title Emperor De, and that his consort be titled Empress Si.
entries.literal: De is for perfect centrality and harmony, si for pure unity of virtue and the Way—we request the posthumous honorific title Emperor De for the eighth-generation imperial ancestor, and Empress Si for his consort.

entries.zh: 好和不爭曰'安'，好廉自克曰'節'，請上皇七代祖尊諡曰安皇帝，妣曰節皇后。
entries.en: An is for loving harmony and not contending, jie for loving integrity and restraining oneself—we ask that the seventh-generation imperial ancestor receive the posthumous title Emperor An, and that his consort be titled Empress Jie.
entries.literal: An is for loving harmony and not contending, jie for loving integrity and restraining oneself—we request the posthumous honorific title Emperor An for the seventh-generation imperial ancestor, and Empress Jie for his consort.

entries.zh: 安民治古曰'定'，明德有勞曰'昭'，尊賢讓善曰'恭'，柔德好眾曰'靖'，請上皇六代祖尊諡曰定昭皇帝，廟號獻祖，妣曰恭靖皇后。
entries.en: Ding is for settling the people and governing by ancient models, zhao for illustrious virtue with meritorious toil, gong for honoring the worthy and yielding to the good, jing for gentle virtue and love of the multitude—we ask that the sixth-generation imperial ancestor receive the posthumous title Emperor Dingzhao, with the temple name Xianzu, and that his consort be titled Empress Gongjing.
entries.literal: Ding is for settling the people and governing by ancient models, zhao for illustrious virtue with meritorious toil, gong for honoring the worthy and yielding to the good, jing for gentle virtue and love of the multitude—we request the posthumous honorific title Emperor Dingzhao for the sixth-generation imperial ancestor, with the temple name Xianzu, and Empress Gongjing for his consort.

entries.zh: 愛民立政曰'成'，辟土有德曰'襄'，強毅執正曰'威'，慈仁和民曰'順'，請上皇五代祖孛堇尊諡曰成襄皇帝，廟號昭祖，妣曰威順皇后。
entries.en: Cheng is for loving the people and establishing government, xiang for opening territory with virtue, wei for firm resolve and upholding rectitude, shun for benevolent harmony and concord with the people—we ask that the fifth-generation imperial ancestor Boqin receive the posthumous title Emperor Chengxiang, with the temple name Zhaozu, and that his consort be titled Empress Weishun.
entries.literal: Cheng is for loving the people and establishing government, xiang for opening territory with virtue, wei for firm resolve and upholding rectitude, shun for benevolent harmony and concord with the people—we request the posthumous honorific title Emperor Chengxiang for the fifth-generation imperial ancestor Boqin, with the temple name Zhaozu, and Empress Weishun for his consort.

entries.zh: 愛民好與曰'惠'，辟土兼國曰'桓'，明德有勞曰'昭'，執心決斷曰'肅'，請上皇高祖太師尊諡曰惠桓皇帝，廟號景祖，妣曰昭肅皇后。
entries.en: Hui is for loving the people and delighting in giving, huan for opening territory and uniting states, zhao for illustrious virtue with meritorious toil, su for firm resolve and decisive judgment—we ask that the imperial great-great-grandfather, Grand Preceptor, receive the posthumous title Emperor Huihuan, with the temple name Jingzu, and that his consort be titled Empress Zhaosu.
entries.literal: Hui is for loving the people and delighting in giving, huan for opening territory and uniting states, zhao for illustrious virtue with meritorious toil, su for firm resolve and decisive judgment—we request the posthumous honorific title Emperor Huihuan for the imperial great-grandfather, Grand Preceptor, with the temple name Jingzu, and Empress Zhaosu for his consort.

entries.zh: 大而化之曰'聖'，剛德克就曰'肅'，思慮深遠曰'翼'，一德不懈曰'簡'，請上皇曾祖太師尊諡曰聖肅皇帝，廟號世祖，妣曰翼簡皇后。
entries.en: Sheng is for great transformation of all under Heaven, su for firm virtue brought to completion, yi for deep thought and far-reaching consideration, jian for single-minded virtue without slackening—we ask that the imperial great-grandfather, Grand Preceptor, receive the posthumous title Emperor Shengsu, with the temple name Shizu, and that his consort be titled Empress Yijian.
entries.literal: Sheng is for great transformation of all under Heaven, su for firm virtue brought to completion, yi for deep thought and far-reaching consideration, jian for single-minded virtue without slackening—we request the posthumous honorific title Emperor Shengsu for the imperial great-great-grandfather, Grand Preceptor, with the temple name Shizu, and Empress Yijian for his consort.

entries.zh: 申情見貌曰'穆'，博聞多能曰'憲'，柔德好眾曰'靜'，聖善周聞曰'宣'，請上皇曾叔祖太師尊諡曰穆憲皇帝，廟號肅宗，妣曰靜宣皇后。
entries.en: Mu is for expressing feeling and revealing true character, xian for broad learning and many abilities, jing for gentle virtue and love of the multitude, xuan for sagely goodness known throughout the realm—we ask that the imperial great-granduncle, Grand Preceptor, receive the posthumous title Emperor Muxian, with the temple name Suzong, and that his consort be titled Empress Jingxuan.
entries.literal: Mu is for expressing feeling and revealing true character, xian for broad learning and many abilities, jing for gentle virtue and love of the multitude, xuan for sagely goodness known throughout the realm—we request the posthumous honorific title Emperor Muxian for the imperial great-great-granduncle, Grand Preceptor, with the temple name Suzong, and Empress Jingxuan for his consort.

entries.zh: 慈愛忘勞曰'孝'，執事有制曰'平'，清白守節曰'貞'，愛民好與曰'惠'，請上皇曾叔祖太師尊諡曰孝平皇帝，廟號穆宗，妣曰貞惠皇后。
entries.en: Xiao is for loving kindness that forgets fatigue, ping for conducting affairs with proper measure, zhen for pure integrity and guarding one's principles, hui for loving the people and delighting in giving—we ask that the imperial great-granduncle, Grand Preceptor, receive the posthumous title Emperor Xiaoping, with the temple name Muzong, and that his consort be titled Empress Zhenhui.
entries.literal: Xiao is for loving kindness that forgets fatigue, ping for conducting affairs with proper measure, zhen for pure integrity and guarding one's principles, hui for loving the people and delighting in giving—we request the posthumous honorific title Emperor Xiaoping for the imperial great-great-granduncle, Grand Preceptor, with the temple name Muzong, and Empress Zhenhui for his consort.

entries.zh: 愛民長悌曰'恭'，一德不懈曰'簡'，夙夜共事 曰'敬'，小心畏忌曰'僖'，請上皇伯祖太師尊諡曰恭簡皇帝，廟號康宗、妣曰敬僖皇后。
entries.en: Gong is for loving the people and long practicing fraternal duty, jian for single-minded virtue without slackening, jing for toiling from dawn to dusk in service, xi for cautious reverence and restraint—we ask that the imperial granduncle, Grand Preceptor, receive the posthumous title Emperor Gongjian, with the temple name Kangzong, and that his consort be titled Empress Jingxi.
entries.literal: Gong is for loving the people and long practicing fraternal duty, jian for single-minded virtue without slackening, jing for toiling from dawn to dusk in service, xi for cautious reverence and restraint—we request the posthumous honorific title Emperor Gongjian for the imperial granduncle, Grand Preceptor, with the temple name Kangzong, and Empress Jingxi for his consort.

entries.zh: 仍請以始祖景元皇帝、景祖惠桓皇帝、世祖聖肅皇帝、太祖武元皇帝、太宗文烈皇帝為永永不祧之廟。
entries.en: We further ask that the Founder Emperor Jingyuan, Jingzu Emperor Huihuan, Shizu Emperor Shengsu, Taizu Emperor Wuyuan, and Taizong Emperor Wenlie be designated as temples that shall never be removed from the main ancestral line.
entries.literal: We further request that the Founder Emperor Jingyuan, Jingzu Emperor Huihuan, Shizu Emperor Shengsu, Taizu Emperor Wuyuan, and Taizong Emperor Wenlie be established as temples never to be displaced from the main line of descent.

entries.zh: 須廟室告成，涓日備物，奉上寶冊，藏于天府，施之罔極。」
entries.en: When the temple chambers are completed, on an appointed day all ritual objects shall be prepared, the precious registers presented, stored in the Heavenly Repository, and their benefit extended without end.'
entries.literal: When the temple chambers are completed, on a chosen day all objects shall be prepared, the precious registers presented, stored in the Heavenly Repository, and applied without limit.'

entries.zh: 丙辰，奉上九代祖妣尊諡廟號，是日百僚上表稱賀。
entries.en: On the bingchen day the court presented posthumous titles and temple names for the nine generations of ancestors and consorts; that same day the officials submitted memorials of congratulation.
entries.literal: On the bingchen day, posthumous honorific titles and temple names for the nine generations of imperial ancestors and consorts were presented; on that day the hundred officials submitted memorials of congratulation.

entries.zh: 是歲閏十一月，增上祖宗尊諡，始祖景元皇帝曰懿憲景元皇帝，德皇帝曰淵穆玄德皇帝，安皇帝曰和靖慶安皇帝，獻祖定昭皇帝曰純烈定昭皇帝，昭祖成襄皇帝曰武惠成襄皇帝，景祖惠桓皇帝曰英烈惠桓皇帝，世祖聖肅皇帝曰神武聖肅皇帝，肅宗穆憲皇帝曰明睿穆憲皇帝，穆宗孝平皇帝曰章順孝平皇帝，康宗恭簡皇帝曰獻敏恭簡皇帝，太宗文烈皇帝曰體元應運世德昭功哲惠仁聖文烈皇帝，徽宗景宣皇帝曰允恭克讓孝德玄功佑聖景宣皇帝，已上廟號如故。
entries.en: In the intercalary eleventh month of that year the court augmented the posthumous titles of the imperial ancestors: Founder Emperor Jingyuan became Emperor Yixian Jingyuan; Emperor De became Emperor Yuanmu Xuande; Emperor An became Emperor Hejing Qing'an; Xianzu Emperor Dingzhao became Emperor Chunlie Dingzhao; Zhaozu Emperor Chengxiang became Emperor Wuhui Chengxiang; Jingzu Emperor Huihuan became Emperor Yinglie Huihuan; Shizu Emperor Shengsu became Emperor Shenwu Shengsu; Suzong Emperor Muxian became Emperor Mingrui Muxian; Muzong Emperor Xiaoping became Emperor Zhangshun Xiaoping; Kangzong Emperor Gongjian became Emperor Xianmin Gongjian; Taizong Emperor Wenlie became Emperor Tiyuan Yingyun Shide Zhaogong Zhehui Rensheng Wenlie; Huizong Emperor Jingxuan became Emperor Yungong Kerang Xiaode Xuangong Yousheng Jingxuan—the temple names listed above remained unchanged.
entries.literal: In the intercalary eleventh month of that year, augmented honorific titles were conferred upon the imperial ancestors: the Founder Emperor Jingyuan became Emperor Yixian Jingyuan; Emperor De became Emperor Yuanmu Xuande; Emperor An became Emperor Hejing Qing'an; Xianzu Emperor Dingzhao became Emperor Chunlie Dingzhao; Zhaozu Emperor Chengxiang became Emperor Wuhui Chengxiang; Jingzu Emperor Huihuan became Emperor Yinglie Huihuan; Shizu Emperor Shengsu became Emperor Shenwu Shengsu; Suzong Emperor Muxian became Emperor Mingrui Muxian; Muzong Emperor Xiaoping became Emperor Zhangshun Xiaoping; Kangzong Emperor Gongjian became Emperor Xianmin Gongjian; Taizong Emperor Wenlie became Emperor Tiyuan Yingyun Shide Zhaogong Zhehui Rensheng Wenlie; Huizong Emperor Jingxuan became Emperor Yungong Kerang Xiaode Xuangong Yousheng Jingxuan—the temple names above remained as before.

entries.zh: 十二月一日，奏告如儀。
entries.en: On the first day of the twelfth month memorial announcements were presented according to ritual.
entries.literal: On the first day of the twelfth month, memorial announcements were presented according to the rite.

entries.zh: 大定二十九年四月乙丑，諡大行皇帝曰光天興運文德武功聖明仁孝皇帝，廟號世宗。
entries.en: On the yichou day of the fourth month, Dading 29, the late emperor received the posthumous title Emperor Guangtian Xingyun Wende Wugong Shengming Renxiao, with the temple name Shizong.
entries.literal: On the yichou day of the fourth month of the twenty-ninth year of Dading, the late emperor was given the posthumous title Emperor Guangtian Xingyun Wende Wugong Shengming Renxiao, with the temple name Shizong.

entries.zh: 五月丙午，以祔廟禮成，大赦。
entries.en: On the bingwu day of the fifth month, with the enshrinement rite complete, the court proclaimed a general amnesty.
entries.literal: On the bingwu day of the fifth month, because the enshrinement rite was completed, a general amnesty was proclaimed.

entries.zh: 大定二十九年五月甲午，上皇考尊諡曰體道弘仁英文睿德光孝皇帝，廟號顯宗。
entries.en: On the jiawu day of the fifth month, Dading 29, the late emperor's father received the posthumous title Emperor Tidao Hongren Yingwen Ruide Guangxiao, with the temple name Xianzong.
entries.literal: On the jiawu day of the fifth month of the twenty-ninth year of Dading, the deceased father was given the posthumous honorific title Emperor Tidao Hongren Yingwen Ruide Guangxiao, with the temple name Xianzong.

entries.zh: 大定元年二月丁卯，諡大行皇帝曰憲天光運仁文義武神聖英孝皇帝，廟號章宗。
entries.en: On the dingmao day of the second month, Dading 1, the late emperor received the posthumous title Emperor Xiantian Guangyun Renwen Yiwu Shensheng Yingxiao, with the temple name Zhangzong.
entries.literal: On the dingmao day of the second month of the first year of Dading, the late emperor was given the posthumous title Emperor Xiantian Guangyun Renwen Yiwu Shensheng Yingxiao, with the temple name Zhangzong.

entries.zh: 正大元年正月戊戌，諡大行皇帝曰繼天興統述道勤仁英武聖孝皇帝，廟號宣宗。
entries.en: On the wuxu day of the first month, Zhengda 1, the late emperor received the posthumous title Emperor Jitian Xingtong Shudao Qinren Yingwu Shengxiao, with the temple name Xuanzong.
entries.literal: On the wuxu day of the first month of the first year of Zhengda, the late emperor was given the posthumous title Emperor Jitian Xingtong Shudao Qinren Yingwu Shengxiao, with the temple name Xuanzong.

entries.zh: 大定三年，增上睿宗尊諡。
entries.en: In Dading 3 the court augmented Ruizong's posthumous title.
entries.literal: In the third year of Dading, Ruizong's honorific title was augmented.

entries.zh: 先是，元年十一月十六日，追冊皇考曰簡肅皇帝，廟號睿宗，皇妣蒲察氏欽慈皇后，皇妣李氏貞懿皇后。
entries.en: Earlier, on the sixteenth day of the eleventh month of the first year, the late emperor's father was posthumously enshrined as Emperor Jiansu, with the temple name Ruizong; his mother of the Pucha clan was titled Empress Qinci, and his mother of the Li clan was titled Empress Zhenyi.
entries.literal: Previously, on the sixteenth day of the eleventh month of the first year, the deceased father was posthumously enshrined as Emperor Jiansu, with the temple name Ruizong; the deceased mother of the Pucha clan was titled Empress Qinci, and the deceased mother of the Li clan was titled Empress Zhenyi.

entries.zh: 二年八月一日，有司奏：「祖宗諡號或十六字，或十四字，或十二字，即今睿宗皇帝更合增上尊諡，於升祔前奉冊寶。」
entries.en: On the first day of the eighth month of the second year the relevant offices memorialized: 'The posthumous titles of the imperial ancestors run to sixteen, fourteen, or twelve characters; Emperor Ruizong should now receive an augmented posthumous title, with registers and seals presented before he is enshrined in the main ancestral line.'
entries.literal: On the first day of the eighth month of the second year, the relevant offices memorialized: 'The honorific titles of the imperial ancestors are either sixteen characters, fourteen characters, or twelve characters in length; Emperor Ruizong should now receive an augmented honorific title, with registers and seals presented before his enshrinement in the main ancestral line.'

entries.zh: 制可。
entries.en: The edict approved it.
entries.literal: An edict approved this.

entries.zh: 十七日，左平章元宜等奏請增上尊諡曰睿宗立德顯仁啟聖廣運文武簡肅皇帝。
entries.en: On the seventeenth day Left Chief Councillor Yuan Yi and others memorialized, asking that the augmented posthumous title be Emperor Ruizong Lide Xianren Qisheng Guangyun Wenwu Jiansu.
entries.literal: On the seventeenth day, Left Chief Councillor Yuan Yi and others memorialized requesting that the augmented honorific title be Ruizong Lide Xianren Qisheng Guangyun Wenwu Jiansu Emperor.

entries.zh: 有司奏：「睿宗皇帝未經升祔，合無于衍慶宮聖武殿設神禦床案？」
entries.en: The relevant offices memorialized: 'Emperor Ruizong has not yet been enshrined in the main ancestral line; should a spirit couch and table be set up in the Shengwu Hall of Yanqing Palace?'
entries.literal: The relevant offices memorialized: 'Emperor Ruizong has not yet been enshrined in the main ancestral line; should a spirit couch and table be set up in the Shengwu Hall of Yanging Palace?'

entries.zh: 奉旨崇聖閣借設正位。
entries.en: By imperial order the principal seat was borrowed from the Chong Sheng Pavilion.
entries.literal: By imperial order the principal seat was borrowed from the Chong Sheng Pavilion for the setup.

entries.zh: 又奏：「皇帝親授冊寶，太尉行事。」
entries.en: They memorialized again: 'The emperor shall personally present the registers and seals, and the Grand Mentor shall conduct the rite.'
entries.literal: They memorialized again: 'The emperor shall personally present the registers and seals, and the Grand Mentor shall conduct the rite.'

entries.zh: 制可。
