entries.literal: Baijia galloped into Shaan and posted a notice to the prefectural populace, saying: "Enemy forces have leaked through from Huainan; fearing they may come by way of Tong Pass, the position cannot be held. County towns are to move into the great cities; grain and baggage are to be gathered at Shaanzhou; those near the mountains are to enter stockaded strongholds to avoid the troops."

entries.zh: 會阿裏合傳旨召兀典入援，兀典遂與潼關總帥納合合閏、秦藍總帥都點檢完顏重喜、安平都尉苗秀、蕩寇都尉術甲某、振武都尉張翼及虎威、鷹揚、葭州劉趙二帥，軍十有一萬、騎五千，盡撒秦藍諸隘之備。
entries.en: Just then Aliha relayed an imperial order summoning Wudian to reinforce the capital. Wudian assembled Tong Pass commander-in-chief Nahan Hehun, Qin-Lan overall commander and chief inspector Wanyan Chongxi, commandants Miao Xiu of Anping, Shujia Mou of Bandit-Suppression, and Zhang Yi of Zhenwu, along with the Tiger Might, Eagle Soar, and the Liu and Zhao commanders of Jia Prefecture—eleven thousand foot soldiers and five thousand horsemen—and stripped all the pass defenses in Qin and Lan.
entries.literal: It happened that Aliha transmitted an edict summoning Wudian to reinforce the capital. Wudian then joined with Tong Pass commander-in-chief Nahan Hehun, Qin-Lan overall commander and chief inspector Wanyan Chongxi, Anping commandant Miao Xiu, Bandit-Suppression commandant Shujia Mou, Zhenwu commandant Zhang Yi, and the Tiger Might, Eagle Soar, and the two commanders Liu and Zhao of Jia Prefecture—eleven thousand infantry and five thousand cavalry—and completely withdrew the defenses of all passes in Qin and Lan.

entries.zh: 從虢入陝。
entries.en: They entered Shaanzhou from Guo Prefecture.
entries.literal: He entered Shaan from Guo.

entries.zh: 同、華、閿鄉一帶軍糧數十萬斛，備關船二百餘艘，皆順流東下。
entries.en: Several hundred thousand hu of military grain in the Tong, Hua, and Minxiang region, along with more than two hundred supply boats, were all sent downstream to the east.
entries.literal: In the Tong, Hua, and Minxiang region military grain amounted to several hundred thousand hu; more than two hundred pass-defense boats were prepared—all went downstream to the east.

entries.zh: 俄聞大兵近，糧皆不及載，船悉空下。
entries.en: Soon word came that the Mongol army was near. There was no time to load the grain, and the boats sailed downstream empty.
entries.literal: Shortly they heard the great army was near; the grain could not all be loaded in time, and the boats all went down empty.

entries.zh: 複盡起州民，連靈寶、硤石倉粟，遊騎至，殺掠不勝計。
entries.en: They mobilized the entire prefectural population and emptied the granaries of Lingbao and Xiaoshi as well. When Mongol scouting parties arrived, the killing and plundering were beyond reckoning.
entries.literal: They again mobilized all the prefectural populace, linking the granaries of Lingbao and Xiaoshi; when roaming cavalry arrived, the killing and plundering were beyond counting.

entries.zh: 又遣陝州觀察副使兼規措轉運副使抹撚速也以船八十往運潼關、閿鄉糧，行及靈寶北河夾灘。
entries.en: They also sent Shaanzhou assistant surveillance commissioner and concurrent assistant transport commissioner Mo'nian Suoye with eighty boats to transport grain from Tong Pass and Minxiang. The convoy reached the narrows of the northern river at Lingbao.
entries.literal: They also dispatched Shaanzhou assistant surveillance commissioner and concurrent assistant transport planning commissioner Mo'nian Suoye with eighty boats to transport grain from Tong Pass and Minxiang; they reached the narrows of the northern river at Lingbao.

entries.zh: 義軍張信、侯三集壯士三百余，保老幼，立水柵。
entries.en: Volunteer commanders Zhang Xin and Hou San rallied more than three hundred stalwarts to protect the elderly and children and erected a water barrier.
entries.literal: Volunteer forces Zhang Xin and Hou San gathered more than three hundred stalwarts, protected the old and young, and erected a water barrier.

entries.zh: 北將忽魯罕只乘淺攻之不能克，遇速也船至即降，大兵得此船遂破侯、張，殺戮殆盡。
entries.en: The Mongol general Huluhazi attacked at the shallows but could not break through. When Suoye's boats arrived he surrendered immediately. The Mongols seized those boats, overran Hou and Zhang's force, and slaughtered nearly everyone.
entries.literal: The northern general Huluhazi attacked at the shallows but could not overcome them. When Suoye's boats arrived he surrendered at once; the great army obtained these boats and then broke Hou and Zhang, slaughtering nearly all.

entries.zh: 初，兀典發閿鄉，拜天，賞軍，人白金三兩，將校有差。
entries.en: When Wudian first set out from Minxiang, he worshipped Heaven and rewarded the troops—three taels of silver per soldier, with graded amounts for officers.
entries.literal: At the outset, when Wudian set out from Minxiang, he worshipped Heaven and rewarded the army—three taels of silver per man, with differences for officers.

entries.zh: 州之庫藏，軍資器械，為之一空。
entries.en: The prefectural treasuries and all military stores and equipment were emptied.
entries.literal: The prefecture's treasuries and military stores and equipment were emptied by this.

entries.zh: 期日進發，已而不行，日造銀器及兵幕牌印，陝州及鹽司牌亦奪取之。
entries.en: A departure date was set, yet they did not march. Day after day Wudian had silver vessels, military tent plaques, and seals manufactured, and he seized the official plaques of Shaanzhou and the Salt Commission as well.
entries.literal: A day was set for advance, yet afterward they did not move; day by day silver vessels and military tent plaques and seals were made, and the plaques of Shaanzhou and the Salt Commission were also seized.

entries.zh: 又欲卻州民財物以資軍，素蘭諫之而止。
entries.en: He also planned to seize civilian property to fund the army, but Sulan's remonstrance put a stop to it.
entries.literal: He also wished to take back the populace's goods and property to supply the army; Sulan remonstrated and it was stopped.

entries.zh: 二月戊午，乃行。
entries.en: On the wuwu day of the second month they finally set out.
entries.literal: On the wuwu day of the second month, they finally marched.

entries.zh: 有李先生者諫曰：「方今大兵俱在河南，河北空虛，相公可先取衛州，出其不意。
entries.en: A certain Master Li remonstrated: "The Mongol army is now entirely in Henan, and Hebei lies empty. Your Excellency could seize Weizhou first and take them by surprise.
entries.literal: A certain Master Li remonstrated, saying: "At present the great army is all in Henan; Hebei is empty. Your Excellency could first take Weizhou by surprise.

entries.zh: 彼知我軍在北，必分兵北渡，京師即得少寬，相公入援亦易為矣。」
entries.en: Once they learn our army is in the north, they will have to divide their forces to cross the river, giving the capital some breathing room and making your relief march far easier."
entries.literal: When they know our army is in the north, they will certainly divide forces to cross north; the capital will gain some relief, and Your Excellency's relief mission will also be easier."

entries.zh: 兀典大怒，以為泄軍機，斬之於市，遂行。
entries.en: Wudian flew into a rage, accused him of leaking military secrets, and had him executed in the marketplace before marching on.
entries.literal: Wudian was greatly enraged, believing he had leaked military secrets, and executed him in the marketplace; then they marched.

entries.zh: 軍士各以老幼自隨。
entries.en: Every soldier brought his elderly dependents and children along.
entries.literal: Each soldier brought old and young dependents along.

entries.zh: 州中亦有關中、河中遷避商賈老幼，亦倚兵力從行，婦女皆嫁士卒，軍中亦有強娶奪者。
entries.en: Merchants and their families who had fled from Guanzhong and Hezhong also joined the column, trusting in military protection. Women were married off to soldiers, and some soldiers seized wives by force.
entries.literal: In the prefecture there were also merchants and their old and young who had fled from Guanzhong and Hezhong; they too relied on military strength to go along. Women were all given in marriage to soldiers, and in the army there were also those who seized wives by force.

entries.zh: 是日，軍出兩東門及南門，不遵洛陽路，乃由州西南徑入大山冰雪中。
entries.en: That day the army marched out through both eastern gates and the southern gate, avoiding the Luoyang road and plunging southwest from the prefecture straight into snowbound mountains.
entries.literal: That day the army went out through both eastern gates and the southern gate, not following the Luoyang road but entering directly into the great mountains and snow and ice by way of the prefecture's southwest.

entries.zh: 葭州劉、趙兩帥即日叛去，大兵以數百騎遙躡其後。
entries.en: The Liu and Zhao commanders of Jia Prefecture defected that same day. Several hundred Mongol horsemen trailed the column at a distance.
entries.literal: The Liu and Zhao commanders of Jia Prefecture defected that very day; the great army followed at a distance with several hundred horsemen.

entries.zh: 明日，張翼軍叛往硃陽，入鹿盧關，大兵追及降之。
entries.en: The next day Zhang Yi's force defected toward Zhuyang and entered Lulu Pass. The Mongols caught up and accepted their surrender.
entries.literal: The next day Zhang Yi's army defected toward Zhuyang, entered Lulu Pass, and when the great army caught up they surrendered.

entries.zh: 山路積雪，晝日凍釋，泥淖及脛，隨軍婦女棄擲幼稚，哀號盈路。
entries.en: Snow lay deep on the mountain paths. By day it thawed and refroze, mud reaching to the shins. Women in the column abandoned their infants, and wailing filled the road.
entries.literal: Snow lay deep on the mountain road; by day it thawed and froze again, mud reaching to the shins. Women following the army abandoned infants; wailing filled the road.

entries.zh: 軍至鐵嶺，大兵潛召洛陽大軍從西三縣過盧氏，所至燒官民廬舍積聚，慮為金軍所據，又反守鐵嶺，以斷歸路。
entries.en: When the Jin army reached Tieling, the Mongols secretly summoned their Luoyang forces through the three western counties via Lushi. Wherever they went they burned official and civilian buildings and stores lest the Jin seize them, then turned back to hold Tieling and cut off the retreat.
entries.literal: When the army reached Tieling, the great army secretly summoned the Luoyang forces to pass through the three western counties via Lushi; wherever they went they burned official and civilian dwellings and stores, fearing the Jin army would seize them; they also turned back to hold Tieling and cut off the route of retreat.

entries.zh: 金兵知必死，皆有鬥志，然已數日不食，行二百里許，困憊不支，頗亦散走。
entries.en: The Jin soldiers knew they faced certain death and fought with desperate resolve, but they had not eaten for days. After marching some two hundred li they collapsed from exhaustion, and many scattered in flight.
entries.literal: The Jin troops knew they must die and all had fighting spirit, yet they had not eaten for several days; after marching some two hundred li they were exhausted beyond endurance and many also scattered and fled.

entries.zh: 於是完顏重喜先降，大軍斬于馬前。
entries.en: Wanyan Chongxi was the first to surrender, and the Mongols beheaded him before their horses.
entries.literal: Thereupon Wanyan Chongxi surrendered first, and the great army beheaded him before their horses.

entries.zh: 鄭倜劫苗英降，英不從，殺之，攜其首以降，於是士卒大潰。
entries.en: Zheng Tong tried to force Miao Ying to surrender. Ying refused and was killed. Tong carried Ying's head to the Mongols and surrendered, and the army collapsed in rout.
entries.literal: Zheng Tong seized Miao Ying to force his surrender; Ying refused and was killed. Tong carried his head to surrender, and then the soldiers collapsed in great rout.

entries.zh: 兀典、合閏提數十騎走山間，追騎禽得，皆殺之。
entries.en: Wudian and Hehun fled through the mountains with several dozen horsemen. Pursuers overtook and captured them, and both were executed.
entries.literal: Wudian and Hehun took several dozen horsemen and fled through the mountains; pursuing riders captured them and all were killed.

entries.zh: 先是，兀典嘗為鄧州節度使，世襲謀克黃摑三合時為宣差都總領，與兀典親厚，故決計入鄧。
entries.en: Wudian had previously served as military commissioner of Dengzhou. The hereditary commander Huangzha Sanheshi, then imperial commissioner and overall chief, was on close terms with him, which is why the army resolved to march toward Deng.
entries.literal: Earlier, Wudian had once been military commissioner of Dengzhou; the hereditary commander Huangzha Sanheshi was imperial commissioner and overall chief, on intimate terms with Wudian, and therefore the decision was made to enter Deng.

entries.zh: 是役也，安平、蕩寇、鷹揚、振威諸都尉，及西安、金雞等軍，脫走者百才一二。
entries.en: Of the Anping, Bandit-Suppression, Eagle Soar, and Zhenwei commandants and the Xi'an, Golden Rooster, and other units, scarcely one or two in a hundred escaped.
entries.literal: In this campaign, of the Anping, Bandit-Suppression, Eagle Soar, and Zhenwei commandants, and the Xi'an, Golden Rooster, and other forces, only one or two in a hundred escaped.

entries.zh: 徒單兀典
entries.en: Tudan Wudian
entries.literal: Tudan Wudian

entries.zh: 賈邦獻，霍州霍邑縣陳村人也。
entries.en: Jia Bangxian was from Chen Village in Huoyi County, Huozhou.
entries.literal: Jia Bangxian was a native of Chen Village in Huoyi County, Huozhou.

entries.zh: 舉進士第。
entries.en: He passed the jinshi examination.
entries.literal: He passed the jinshi examination.

entries.zh: 質直有勇略。
entries.en: He was upright by nature and possessed courage and strategic sense.
entries.literal: He was upright by nature and possessed courage and strategy.

entries.zh: 大元攻河東，邦獻集居民為守禦計。
entries.en: When Yuan forces attacked Hedong, Bangxian gathered the residents to organize a defense.
entries.literal: When Great Yuan forces attacked Hedong, Bangxian gathered the residents to plan defense.

entries.zh: 既而，兵大至，居民悉降。
entries.en: Before long a large army arrived and the residents all surrendered.
entries.literal: Before long the army arrived in force and the residents all surrendered.

entries.zh: 邦獻棄其家，獨與子懿保于松平寨。
entries.en: Bangxian abandoned his household and alone with his son Yi took refuge at Songping Stockade.
entries.literal: Bangxian abandoned his household and alone with his son Yi took refuge at Songping Stockade.

entries.zh: 是時，權知州事劉珍在寨，與之共守，竟能成功。
entries.en: At that time Liu Zhen, acting prefect, was at the stockade; together they held it and succeeded in the end.
entries.literal: At this time Liu Zhen, acting prefect, was at the stockade; together they defended it and in the end succeeded.

entries.zh: 珍每欲辟之，邦獻輒以衰老為辭。
entries.en: Whenever Zhen wished to recruit him, Bangxian declined on grounds of old age.
entries.literal: Whenever Zhen wished to recruit him, Bangxian declined on the grounds of old age.

entries.zh: 興定四年十月，兵複大至，病不能避，與懿俱被執。
entries.en: In the tenth month of the fourth year of Xingding the army came again in force. Too ill to escape, he and Yi were both captured.
entries.literal: In the tenth month of the fourth year of Xingding the army came again in force; ill and unable to escape, he and Yi were both captured.

entries.zh: 欲以為鎮西元帥，且持刃脅之，邦獻不屈，密遣懿歸松平，遂自剄。
entries.en: They wished to make him Marshal of the West and threatened him with blades. Bangxian refused, secretly sent Yi back to Songping, and cut his own throat.
entries.literal: They wished to make him Marshal of the West and moreover threatened him with blades; Bangxian would not submit, secretly sent Yi back to Songping, and then cut his own throat.

entries.zh: 贈奉直大夫、本縣令。
entries.en: He was posthumously made Grand Master of Direct Service and magistrate of his home county.
entries.literal: He was posthumously awarded Grand Master of Direct Service and Magistrate of his home county.

entries.zh: 列傳第六十 忠義二 ○吳僧哥 烏古論德升 張順 馬驤 伯德窊哥 奧屯醜和尚 從坦 孛朮魯福壽 吳邦傑 納合蒲剌都 女奚烈斡出 時茂先 溫蒂罕老兒 梁持勝 賈邦獻 移剌阿里合 完顏六斤 紇石烈鶴壽 蒲察婁室 女奚烈資祿 趙益 侯小叔 王佐 黃摑九住 烏林答乞住 陀滿斜烈 尼厖古蒲魯虎 兀顏畏可 兀顏訛出虎 粘割貞
entries.en: Biographies 60: Loyalty and Righteousness II — Wu Sengge, Wugulun Desheng, Zhang Shun, Ma Xiang, Bode Wage, Aotun Chouheshang, Cong Tan, Beipailu Fushou, Wu Bangjie, Nahe Puladu, Nuxilie Wochu, Shi Maoxian, Wendihan Lao'er, Liang Chisheng, Jia Bangxian, Yila Alihe, Wanyan Liujin, Geshilie Heshou, Pucha Loushi, Nuxilie Zilu, Zhao Yi, Hou Xiaoshu, Wang Zuo, Huangguai Jiuzhu, Wulinda Qizhu, Tuoman Xielie, Nilanggupuluhu, Wuyan Weike, Wuyan Echuhu, and Zhange Zhen
entries.literal: Biographies 60: Loyalty and Righteousness II ○ Wu Sengge, Wugulun Desheng, Zhang Shun, Ma Xiang, Bode Wage, Aotun Chouheshang, Cong Tan, Beipailu Fushou, Wu Bangjie, Nahe Puladu, Nuxilie Wochu, Shi Maoxian, Wendihan Lao'er, Liang Chisheng, Jia Bangxian, Yila Alihe, Wanyan Liujin, Geshilie Heshou, Pucha Loushi, Nuxilie Zilu, Zhao Yi, Hou Xiaoshu, Wang Zuo, Huangguai Jiuzhu, Wulinda Qizhu, Tuoman Xielie, Nilanggupuluhu, Wuyan Weike, Wuyan Echuhu, Zhange Zhen

entries.zh: 杜時升，字進之，霸州信安人。
entries.en: Du Shisheng, styled Jinzhi, came from Xin'an in Bazhou.
entries.literal: Du Shisheng, style name Jinzhi, was a native of Xin'an in Bazhou.

entries.zh: 博學知天文，不肯仕進。
entries.en: Broadly learned and versed in astronomy, he refused to seek office.
entries.literal: Broadly learned and versed in astronomy, he refused to seek office.

entries.zh: 承安、泰和間，宰相數薦時升可大用。
entries.en: During Chengan and Taihe, chief ministers repeatedly recommended Shisheng for high office.
entries.literal: During Chengan and Taihe, the chief ministers repeatedly recommended Shisheng for great employment.

entries.zh: 時升謂所親曰：「吾觀正北赤氣如血，東西亙天，天下當大亂，亂而南北當合為一。
entries.en: Shisheng told those close to him, "I see crimson vapor like blood in the far north, stretching east and west across the sky; the realm will fall into great disorder, and when the turmoil ends north and south will become one.
entries.literal: Shisheng said to those close to him: "I observe crimson vapor like blood in the far north, stretching east and west across the sky; the realm will suffer great disorder, and after the disorder north and south will become one.

entries.zh: 消息盈虛，迴圈無端，察往考來，孰能違之。」
entries.en: Growth and decline, fullness and emptiness, cycle without end — who, examining past and future, can defy it?"
entries.literal: Growth and decline, fullness and emptiness, cycle without end — examining past and scrutinizing future, who can defy this?"

entries.zh: 是時，風俗侈靡，紀綱大壞，世宗之業遂衰。
entries.en: At that time customs were extravagant and corrupt, institutions were in ruins, and the achievements of Emperor Shizong went into decline.
entries.literal: At that time customs were extravagant and corrupt, the laws were greatly broken down, and the achievements of Emperor Shizong declined.

entries.zh: 時升乃南渡河，隱居嵩、洛山中，從學者甚眾。
entries.en: Shisheng then crossed the river south, withdrew to the Song and Luo mountains, and attracted a great many students.
entries.literal: Shisheng then crossed the river south, withdrew to the Song and Luo mountains, and had very many students.

entries.zh: 大抵以「伊洛之學」教人自時升始。
entries.en: Teaching the "learning of the Yi and Luo" broadly to others began with Shisheng.
entries.literal: Teaching people broadly with the "learning of the Yi and Luo" began with Shisheng.

entries.zh: 正大間，大元兵攻潼關，拒守甚堅，眾皆相賀，時升曰：「大兵皆在秦、鞏間，若假道于宋，出襄、漢入宛、葉，鐵騎長驅勢如風雨，無高山大川為之阻，土崩之勢也。」
entries.en: During Zhengda, when the Great Yuan army attacked Tong Pass and the defense held firm, all congratulated one another; Shisheng said, "The main force is all between Qin and Gong; if they borrow a route through Song, emerge from Xiang and Han into Wan and Ye, and iron cavalry drives straight ahead like wind and rain with no high mountains or great rivers to block them, the realm will collapse like a landslide."
entries.literal: During Zhengda, when the Great Yuan army attacked Tong Pass and the defense was very firm, all congratulated one another; Shisheng said: "The great army is all between Qin and Gong; if it borrows a route through Song, emerges from Xiang and Han into Wan and Ye, and iron cavalry drives straight ahead like wind and rain with no high mountains or great rivers to obstruct them, it will be a landslide collapse."

entries.zh: 頃之，大元兵果自饒峰關涉襄陽出南陽，金人敗績於三峰山，汴京不守，皆如時升所料雲。
entries.en: Before long the Great Yuan army did cross Raofeng Pass through Xiangyang and emerge at Nanyang; the Jin were defeated at Sanfeng Mountain and Bianjing fell — all exactly as Shisheng had foreseen.
entries.literal: Before long the Great Yuan army indeed crossed Raofeng Pass through Xiangyang and emerged at Nanyang; the Jin suffered defeat at Sanfeng Mountain, Bianjing could not be held — all as Shisheng had foreseen.

entries.zh: 正大末，卒。
entries.en: In the late Zhengda era he died.
entries.literal: In the late Zhengda era he died.

entries.zh: 辛願，字敬之，福昌人。
entries.en: Xin Yuan, styled Jingzhi, came from Fuchang.
entries.literal: Xin Yuan, style name Jingzhi, was a native of Fuchang.

entries.zh: 年二十五始知讀書，取《白氏諷諫集》自試，一日便能背誦。
entries.en: At twenty-five he first learned to read; he took Bai Juyi's Collection of Admonitions and Satires to test himself and could recite it in a single day.
entries.literal: At twenty-five he first learned to read books; he took Bai Juyi's Collection of Admonitions and Satires to test himself and could recite it in a single day.

entries.zh: 乃聚書環堵中讀之，至《書伊訓》、《詩河廣》頗若有所省，欲罷不能，因更致力焉。
entries.en: He then gathered books and read within four walls; when he reached the "Instructions of Yi" in the Documents and "He Guangs" in the Odes he seemed awakened, wished to stop but could not, and redoubled his effort.
entries.literal: He then gathered books and read them within four walls; when he reached the "Instructions of Yi" in the Documents and "He Guangs" in the Odes he seemed somewhat enlightened, wished to stop but could not, and therefore redoubled his effort.

entries.zh: 由是博極書史，作文有繩尺，詩律精嚴有自得之趣。
entries.en: From this he became broadly versed in books and histories; his prose had measure and discipline, and his regulated verse was precise and strict with a flavor uniquely his own.
entries.literal: From this he became broadly versed in books and histories; in prose he had measure and rule, and in regulated verse he was precise and strict with a flavor of self-attainment.

entries.zh: 性野逸，不修威儀，貴人延客，麻衣草屨、足脛赤露坦然於其間，劇談豪飲，傍若無人。
entries.en: Wild and untamed by nature, he did not cultivate imposing bearing; when nobles entertained guests, he appeared among them in hemp robes and straw sandals with bare shins exposed, talked freely and drank boldly, as if no one else were present.
entries.literal: By nature wild and untamed, he did not cultivate imposing bearing; when nobles entertained guests, he would appear among them in hemp robes and straw sandals with bare shins openly exposed, talk freely and drink boldly, as if no one were beside him.

entries.zh: 嘗謂王鬱曰：「王侯將相，世所共嗜者，聖人有以得之亦不避。
entries.en: He once said to Wang Yu, "Kings, marquises, generals, and ministers are what the world commonly covets; if a sage obtains them by proper means he does not avoid them.
entries.literal: He once said to Wang Yu: "Kings, marquises, generals, and ministers are what the world commonly covets; if a sage obtains them by proper means he does not avoid them.

entries.zh: 得之不以道，與夫居之不能行己之志，是欲澡其身而伏於廁也。
entries.en: To obtain them not by the Way, or to hold them yet be unable to carry out one's own aims — that is like wanting to bathe yet crouching in a privy.
entries.literal: To obtain them not by the Way, or to hold them yet be unable to carry out one's own aims — that is like wanting to bathe the body yet crouching in a privy.

entries.zh: 是難與他人道，子宜保之。」
entries.en: This is hard to speak of to others; you should keep it safe."
entries.literal: This is hard to speak of to others; you should keep it safe."

entries.zh: 其志趣如此。
entries.en: His aspirations were of this kind.
entries.literal: His aspirations were of this kind.

entries.zh: 後為河南府治中高廷玉客。
entries.en: Later he became a retainer of Gao Tingyu, administrative aide of Henan Prefecture.
entries.literal: Later he became a retainer of Gao Tingyu, administrative aide of Henan Prefecture.

entries.zh: 廷玉為府尹溫蒂罕福興所誣，願亦被訊掠，幾不得免，自是生事益狼狽。
entries.en: Tingyu was slandered by the prefect Wendihan Fuxing; Yuan was also tortured under interrogation and nearly could not escape; from then on his affairs grew ever more distressed.
entries.literal: Tingyu was slandered by the prefect Wendihan Fuxing; Yuan was also interrogated under torture and nearly could not escape; from then on his affairs grew ever more distressed.

entries.zh: 願雅負高氣，不以從俗俯仰，迫以饑凍流離，往往見之於詩。
entries.en: Yuan bore lofty spirit by nature and would not bow to custom; pressed by hunger, cold, and wandering exile, this often appeared in his poetry.
entries.literal: Yuan by nature bore lofty spirit and would not bow and yield to custom; pressed by hunger, cold, and wandering exile, this often appeared in his poetry.

entries.zh: 有詩數千首，常貯竹橐中。
entries.en: He had several thousand poems, which he always kept in a bamboo bag.
entries.literal: He had several thousand poems, which he always kept in a bamboo bag.

entries.zh: 正大末，歿洛下。
entries.en: In the late Zhengda era he died in the Luo region.
entries.literal: In the late Zhengda era he died below Luo.

entries.zh: 其詩有雲：「黃綺暫來為漢友，巢由終不是唐臣。」
entries.en: Among his poems is the line: "Huang and Qi came for a time as friends of Han; Chao and You in the end were not ministers of Tang."
entries.literal: Among his poems is the line: "Huang and Qi came for a time as friends of Han; Chao and You in the end were not ministers of Tang."

entries.zh: 真處士語也。
entries.en: These are truly the words of a recluse.
entries.literal: These are truly the words of a recluse.

entries.zh: 孝友者，人之至行也，而恆性存焉。
entries.en: Filial devotion and brotherly friendship rank among the highest human virtues, and they embody what is constant in human nature.
entries.literal: Filial piety and fraternal friendship are the utmost conduct of human beings, and within them the constant nature is preserved.

entries.zh: 有子者欲其孝，有弟者欲其友，豈非人之恆情乎？
entries.en: Parents hope their sons will be filial; elder brothers hope their younger brothers will be dutiful — is this not the enduring sentiment common to all people?
entries.literal: Those who have sons desire their filial piety; those who have younger brothers desire their friendship — is this not the constant feeling of human beings?

entries.zh: 為子而孝，為弟而友，又豈非人之恆性乎？
entries.en: To act as a filial son and a devoted younger brother — is this not likewise what is constant in human nature?
entries.literal: To be filial as a son and friendly as a younger brother — is this not again the constant nature of human beings?

entries.zh: 以人之恆情責人之恆性，而不副所欲者恆有焉。
entries.en: When one measures people's constant nature against their constant feelings, there will always be those who fall short of what is hoped for.
entries.literal: Using the constant feelings of people to demand the constant nature of people, those who do not meet what is desired constantly exist.

entries.zh: 有竭力於是，豈非難乎。
entries.en: To strive with one's whole heart toward this end is no easy thing.
entries.literal: To exert one's full strength in this — is it not difficult?

entries.zh: 天生五穀以養人，五穀之有恆性也。
entries.en: Heaven created the five grains to sustain humankind, and the grains themselves possess a fixed nature.
entries.literal: Heaven produced the five grains to nourish people; the five grains have a constant nature.

entries.zh: 服田力穡以望有秋，農夫之有恆情也。
entries.en: To till the soil and labor through the seasons in hope of an autumn harvest is the farmer's unchanging aim.
entries.literal: To work the fields and labor at harvest in hopes of an autumn yield — this is the constant feeling of farmers.

entries.zh: 五穀熟，人民育，豈異事乎。
entries.en: When the grain ripens, the people thrive — are these not one and the same outcome?
entries.literal: When the five grains ripen, the people are nourished — are these different matters?

entries.zh: 然以唐、虞之世，「黎民阻饑」不免以命稷，「百姓不親、五品不遜」不免以命契，以是知順成之不可必，猶孝友之不易得也。
entries.en: Even in the age of Tang and Yu, when "the people were beset by hunger," Ji had to be put in charge of agriculture; when "the common folk were estranged and the five bonds of kinship were in disorder," Qi had to be entrusted with education — which shows that a bountiful harvest cannot be taken for granted any more than filial piety and brotherly devotion can be secured at will.
entries.literal: Yet in the age of Tang and Yu, when it was said that "the black-haired people were obstructed by famine," Ji had to be appointed; when "the common people were not affectionate and the five relations were not in order," Qi had to be appointed — from this one knows that harmonious success cannot be assured, just as filial piety and friendship are not easily obtained.

entries.zh: 是故「有年」、「大有年」以異書于聖人之經，孝友以至行傳于歷代之史，勸農興孝之教不廢於歷代之政，孝弟力田自漢以來有其科。
entries.en: This is why phrases like "a year of abundance" and "a year of great abundance" receive special notice in the classics of the sages, why exemplary filial piety and friendship are recorded generation after generation as supreme virtue, why successive dynasties never ceased to exhort farming and filial duty in their policies, and why the Han and later dynasties maintained stipends for "filial sons and brothers who exert themselves in farming."
entries.literal: Therefore "a good year" and "a great good year" are recorded with special phrasing in the classics of the sages; filial piety and friendship are transmitted in the histories of successive dynasties as the utmost conduct; the teachings of encouraging agriculture and promoting filial piety have never been abandoned in the policies of successive ages; and since the Han there has been the quota for filial sons and brothers who exert themselves in farming.

entries.zh: 章宗嘗曰：「孝義之人，素行已備，雖有希覬，猶不失為行善。」
entries.en: Emperor Zhangzong once remarked: "Those who are filial and righteous have already perfected their daily conduct; even if they harbor some personal ambition, they still count as men who do good."
entries.literal: Emperor Zhangzong once said: "Men of filial piety and righteousness have already perfected their conduct in ordinary life; even if they harbor some ambition, they still do not cease to be men of good deeds."

entries.zh: 庶幾帝王之善訓矣。
entries.en: This may be taken as the worthy teaching of sage emperors.
entries.literal: This is perhaps the good instruction of sage sovereigns.

entries.zh: 夫金世孝友見於旌表、載於史冊者僅六人焉。
entries.en: Under the Jin, only six men whose filial piety and brotherly devotion earned public commendation and a place in the historical record can be named.
entries.literal: In the Jin dynasty, those whose filial piety and friendship were honored with commemorative tablets and recorded in the histories numbered only six.

entries.zh: 作《孝友傳》。
entries.en: Hence this "Biographies of Filial Piety and Friendship."
entries.literal: I compose the "Biographies of Filial Piety and Friendship."

entries.zh: 列傳第六十六 循吏 ○盧克忠 牛德昌 范承吉 王政 張奕 李瞻 劉敏行 傅慎微 劉煥 高昌福 孫德淵 趙鑒 蒲察鄭留 女奚烈守愚 石抹元 張彀 趙重福 武都 紇石烈德 張特立 王浩
entries.en: Biographies 66: Virtuous Officials — Lu Kezhong, Niu Dechang, Fan Chengji, Wang Zheng, Zhang Yi, Li Zhan, Liu Minxing, Fu Shenwei, Liu Huan, Gao Changfu, Sun Deyuan, Zhao Jian, Pucha Zhengliu, Nuxilie Shouyu, Shi Moyuan, Zhang Gou, Zhao Zhongfu, Wu Dou, Geshilie De, Zhang Teli, and Wang Hao
entries.literal: Biographies 66: Virtuous Officials — Lu Kezhong, Niu Dechang, Fan Chengji, Wang Zheng, Zhang Yi, Li Zhan, Liu Minxing, Fu Shenwei, Liu Huan, Gao Changfu, Sun Deyuan, Zhao Jian, Pucha Zhengliu, Nuxilie Shouyu, Shi Moyuan, Zhang Gou, Zhao Zhongfu, Wu Dou, Geshilie De, Zhang Teli, Wang Hao

entries.zh: 張奕，字彥微，其先澤州高平人。
entries.en: Zhang Yi, styled Yanwei, traced his ancestry to Gaoping in Ze Prefecture.
entries.literal: Zhang Yi, courtesy name Yanwei, was descended from Gaoping in Ze Prefecture.

entries.zh: 以廕補官，仕齊為歸德府通判。
entries.en: He entered office through hereditary privilege and served the Qi state as vice prefect of Guide Prefecture.
entries.literal: He entered office through hereditary privilege and served Qi as vice prefect of Guide Prefecture.

entries.zh: 齊國廢，齊兵之在郡者二萬人謀為亂，約夜半舉燎相應。
entries.en: When the Qi state was abolished, the twenty thousand Qi troops still in the prefecture plotted a revolt, agreeing to light beacon fires at midnight as their signal.
entries.literal: When the Qi state was abolished, the twenty thousand Qi soldiers in the prefecture plotted rebellion, agreeing to raise beacon fires at midnight as signals to one another.

entries.zh: 奕知之，選市人丁壯授以兵，結陣扼其要巷，開小南門以示生路，亂不得作，比明亡匿略盡，擒其首惡誅之。
entries.en: Yi learned of the plot, drafted able-bodied men from the market and armed them, formed ranks to hold the key alleys, and opened the Small South Gate to offer an escape route. The revolt never broke out; by dawn most of the conspirators had fled, and Yi seized the ringleaders and executed them.
entries.literal: Yi learned of it, selected able-bodied men from the market and armed them, formed ranks to block the key alleys, and opened the Small South Gate to show an escape route. The rebellion could not break out; by dawn those in hiding had largely fled, and he seized the ringleaders and executed them.

entries.zh: 後五日，都統完顏阿魯補以軍至歸德，欲根株餘黨，奕以闔門保郡人無他，遂止。
entries.en: Five days later Commander Wanyan Alubu arrived at Guide with his army and wanted to root out every last conspirator. Yi pledged his entire household that the people of the prefecture meant no further harm, and the purge was stopped.
entries.literal: Five days later the commander Wanyan Alubu arrived at Guide with his army and wished to root out the remaining conspirators. Yi pledged his entire household that the people of the prefecture had no further designs, and the pursuit was halted.

entries.zh: 行台承制除同知歸德尹。
entries.en: The mobile secretariat, acting under imperial commission, appointed him deputy prefect of Guide.
entries.literal: The mobile secretariat, acting under imperial commission, appointed him deputy prefect of Guide.

entries.zh: 天眷元年，以河南與宋，改同知沂州防禦使事。
entries.en: In the first year of Tianjuan, when Henan was ceded to Song, he was made deputy defender of Yizhou.
entries.literal: In the first year of Tianjuan, when Henan was ceded to Song, he was changed to deputy defender of Yizhou.

entries.zh: 三年，宗弼複取河南，征奕赴行省，既定汴京，授汴京副留守。
entries.en: In the third year Zongbi retook Henan; Yi was summoned to the mobile secretariat, and once Bianjing was secured he was made deputy guardian of Bianjing.
entries.literal: In the third year Zongbi recovered Henan; Yi was summoned to the mobile secretariat, and once Bianjing was secured he was appointed deputy guardian of Bianjing.

entries.zh: 曆陳、秦州防禦使，同知太原尹。
entries.en: He successively served as defender of Chen and Qin prefectures and as deputy metropolitan prefect of Taiyuan.
entries.literal: He successively served as defender of Chen and Qin prefectures and as deputy metropolitan prefect of Taiyuan.

entries.zh: 晉甯軍報夏人侵界，詔奕往征之。
entries.en: The Jinning Army reported a Xia border incursion; the throne ordered Yi to investigate.
entries.literal: The Jinning Army reported that the Xia had invaded the border; an edict ordered Yi to go and investigate.

entries.zh: 奕至境上，按籍各歸所侵土，還奏曰：「折氏世守麟府，以抗夏人。
entries.en: Yi reached the border, checked the registers, and restored each tract of invaded land; on returning he memorialized, "The Zhe clan had held Lin Prefecture for generations to resist the Xia.
entries.literal: Yi reached the border, checked the registers, and returned each tract of invaded land; returning he memorialized: "The Zhe clan for generations held Lin Prefecture to resist the Xia.

entries.zh: 本朝有其地遂以與夏。
entries.en: Our dynasty held that territory and then ceded it to the Xia.
entries.literal: Our dynasty possessed that territory and then gave it to the Xia.

entries.zh: 夏人夷折氏墳壟而戮其屍，折氏怨入骨髓而不得報也。
entries.en: The Xia leveled the Zhe tombs and desecrated their dead; the Zhe clan's hatred ran to the marrow and could not be avenged.
entries.literal: The Xia leveled the Zhe clan's tombs and desecrated their corpses; the Zhe clan's hatred entered to the marrow and could not be avenged.

entries.zh: 今複使守晉寧，故激怒夏人使為鼠侵，而條上其罪，苟欲開邊釁以雪私仇耳。
entries.en: Now they are posted again to guard Jinning, deliberately provoking petty Xia raids while charges are filed against them—this is only to open a border quarrel and settle a private grudge.
entries.literal: Now they are again made to guard Jinning, so the Xia are deliberately provoked into petty incursions, and charges are listed against them—this is merely to open a border quarrel and settle a private grudge.

entries.zh: 獨可徙折氏他郡，則夏人自安。」
entries.en: Move the Zhe clan to another prefecture, and the Xia will settle down of themselves."
entries.literal: They need only be moved to another prefecture, and the Xia will settle of themselves."

entries.zh: 朝廷從之，遂移折氏守青州。
entries.en: The court agreed and transferred the Zhe clan to guard Qingzhou.
entries.literal: The court adopted this and thereupon transferred the Zhe clan to guard Qingzhou.

entries.zh: 正隆間，同知西京留守事，遷河東北路轉運使。
entries.en: During Zhenglong he served as deputy guardian of the Western Capital and was promoted to transport commissioner of the Hedong North Route.
entries.literal: During the Zhenglong era he served as deputy guardian of the Western Capital and was promoted to transport commissioner of the Hedong North Route.

entries.zh: 大定二年，征為戶部尚書，甫視事，得疾卒。
entries.en: In the second year of Dading he was summoned as minister of revenue; he had barely taken office when he fell ill and died.
entries.literal: In the second year of Dading he was summoned as minister of revenue; he had only just taken office when he fell ill and died.

entries.zh: 列傳第六十八 列女 ○阿鄰妻 李寶信妻 韓慶民妻 雷婦師氏 康住住 李文妻 李英妻 相琪妻 阿魯真 撒合輦妻 許古妻 馮妙真 蒲察氏 烏古論氏 素蘭妻 忙哥妻 尹氏 白氏 聶孝女 仲德妻 寶符李氏 張鳳奴
entries.en: Biographies 68 — Exemplary Women: The Wife of A Lin; The Wife of Li Baoxin; The Wife of Han Qingmin; Lei Fu, née Shi; Kang Zhuzhu; The Wife of Li Wen; The Wife of Li Ying; The Wife of Xiang Qi; A Luzhen; The Wife of Sahe Nian; The Wife of Xu Gu; Feng Miaozhen; Lady Pucha; Lady Wugulun; The Wife of Su Lan; The Wife of Mang Ge; Lady Yin; Lady Bai; Nie Xiaonü; The Wife of Zhong De; Lady Li of Baofu; Zhang Fengnu
entries.literal: Biographies 68 — Exemplary Women: Wife of A Lin; Wife of Li Baoxin; Wife of Han Qingmin; Lei Fu, née Shi; Kang Zhuzhu; Wife of Li Wen; Wife of Li Ying; Wife of Xiang Qi; A Luzhen; Wife of Sahe Nian; Wife of Xu Gu; Feng Miaozhen; Lady Pucha; Lady Wugulun; Wife of Su Lan; Wife of Mang Ge; Lady Yin; Lady Bai; Nie Xiaonü; Wife of Zhong De; Lady Li of Baofu; Zhang Fengnu

entries.zh: 李英妻
entries.en: The Wife of Li Ying
entries.literal: Wife of Li Ying

entries.zh: 李英妻張氏。
entries.en: The wife of Li Ying was a woman of the Zhang clan.
entries.literal: The wife of Li Ying was a woman of the Zhang clan.

entries.zh: 英初為監察禦史，在中都，張居濰州。
entries.en: Ying first served as investigating censor at the Central Capital while Zhang remained at Wei Prefecture.
entries.literal: Ying was at first investigating censor; he was at the Central Capital, while Zhang resided at Wei Prefecture.

entries.zh: 貞祐元年冬，大元兵取濰州，入其家，張氏盡以所有財物與之。
entries.en: In the winter of the first year of Zhenyou (1213), Mongol forces took Wei Prefecture, entered her home, and Lady Zhang surrendered everything she owned.
entries.literal: In the winter of the first year of Zhenyou, the Great Yuan army took Wei Prefecture, entered her house, and Lady Zhang gave them all her possessions.

entries.zh: 既而，令張氏上馬，張曰：「我盡以物與汝，猶不見贖邪？」
entries.en: Then they ordered her to mount a horse. She said, "I have given you everything I own—is that still not enough to let me go?"
entries.literal: Presently they ordered Lady Zhang to mount a horse; Zhang said, "I have given you all my goods—do you still not see fit to ransom me?"

entries.zh: 答曰「汝品官妻，當複為夫人。」
entries.en: They replied, "You are a ranked official's wife—you will be a lady again."
entries.literal: They answered, "You are the wife of a ranked official—you shall again become a great lady."

entries.zh: 張曰：「我死則為李氏鬼。」
entries.en: Zhang said, "In death I shall be a ghost of the Li household."
entries.literal: Zhang said, "If I die I shall be a ghost of the Li clan."

entries.zh: 頓坐不起，遂見殺。
entries.en: She sat down and would not rise, and they killed her.
entries.literal: She sat down abruptly and would not rise, and was thereupon killed.

entries.zh: 追封隴西郡夫人，諡「莊潔」。
entries.en: She was posthumously enfeoffed as Lady of Longxi Commandery with the posthumous name "Solemn and Chaste."
entries.literal: She was posthumously enfeoffed as Lady of Longxi Commandery, with the posthumous name "Solemn and Chaste."

entries.zh: 英仕至御史中丞，有傳。
entries.en: Ying rose to censor-in-chief; he has a separate biography.
entries.literal: Ying rose in office to censor-in-chief; he has a biography.

entries.zh: 韓慶民妻者，不知何許人，亦不知其姓氏。
entries.en: The wife of Han Qingmin was a woman of unknown origin and unknown surname.
entries.literal: The wife of Han Qingmin—her native place is unknown, and her surname is also unknown.

entries.zh: 慶民事遼為宜州節度使。
entries.en: Qingmin had served the Liao as military commissioner of Yi Prefecture.
entries.literal: Qingmin served the Liao as military commissioner of Yi Prefecture.

entries.zh: 天會中，攻破宜州，慶民不屈而死，以其妻配將士，其妻誓死不從，遂自殺。
entries.en: During the Tianhui era (1115–1135), when Yi Prefecture fell, Qingmin refused to submit and was put to death; his wife was assigned to the troops, but she swore she would die rather than obey and took her own life.
entries.literal: In the Tianhui era, when Yi Prefecture was taken by assault, Qingmin died unyielding; his wife was allotted to officers and soldiers; she vowed to die rather than submit and thereupon killed herself.

entries.zh: 世宗讀《太宗實錄》，見慶民夫婦事，歎曰：「如此節操，可謂難矣。」
entries.en: When Emperor Shizong read the Veritable Records of Taizong and came upon their story, he sighed and said, "Constancy such as this is truly rare."
entries.literal: Emperor Shizong read the Veritable Records of Taizong, saw the affair of Qingmin and his wife, and sighed, saying, "Such constancy may truly be called rare."

entries.zh: 大定八年，世宗擊球于常武殿，貴中上疏諫曰：「陛下為天下主，守宗廟社稷之重，圍獵擊球皆危事也。
entries.en: In the eighth year of Dading (1168), Emperor Shizong played cuju at the Ever Martial Hall. Guizhong submitted a memorial of remonstrance: "Your Majesty is lord of all under Heaven, charged with the ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain. Hunting and cuju are dangerous pursuits.
entries.literal: In the eighth year of Dading, Emperor Shizong played cuju at the Ever Martial Hall; Guizhong submitted a memorial remonstrating: 'Your Majesty is lord of all under Heaven, guarding the weight of the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain — hunting and cuju are all dangerous affairs.

entries.zh: 前日皇太子墜馬，可以為戒，臣願一切罷之。」
entries.en: The crown prince fell from his horse the other day. Let that be a warning. Your servant begs that all such pastimes be abandoned."
entries.literal: The other day the crown prince fell from his horse — that may serve as a warning; your servant wishes that all such activities be abolished.'

entries.zh: 上曰：「祖宗以武定天下，豈以承平遽忘之邪。
entries.en: The emperor said, "Our ancestors settled the realm by force of arms. How could we forget that now, in a time of peace?
entries.literal: The emperor said: 'Our ancestors settled the realm by arms — how could we in a time of peace suddenly forget that?

entries.zh: 皇統嘗罷此事，當時之人皆以為非，朕所親見，故示天下以習武耳。」
entries.en: Under Huangtong this practice was once abandoned, and everyone at the time thought it a mistake. I saw it myself. I keep these exercises only to show the realm that we still train for war."
entries.literal: During Huangtong this matter was once abolished, and people of that time all thought it wrong — I saw it with my own eyes, and therefore show the realm military training, that is all.'

entries.zh: 十年十一月，皇太子生日，世宗宴百官於東宮。
entries.en: In the eleventh month of the tenth year, on the crown prince's birthday, Shizong gave a feast for the officials at the Eastern Palace.
entries.literal: In the eleventh month of the tenth year, on the crown prince's birthday, Shizong feasted the hundred officials at the Eastern Palace.

entries.zh: 上飲歡甚，貴中被酒，前跪欲言事，錯亂失次，上不之罪，但令扶出。
entries.en: The emperor drank freely. Guizhong, drunk, knelt forward to speak on some matter, grew confused, and lost all decorum. The emperor did not punish him but had him helped out.
entries.literal: The emperor drank with great joy; Guizhong was drunk on wine, came forward kneeling wishing to speak on affairs, became confused and lost order; the emperor did not punish him but only ordered him helped out.

entries.zh: 古之宦者皆出於刑人，刑余不可列於士庶，故掌宮寺之事，謂之「婦寺」焉。
entries.en: In ancient times every eunuch was drawn from the ranks of criminals. Once mutilated by penal law, a man could no longer stand among scholars or the common people, and so he was put in charge of palace affairs — hence the term "palace women attendants."
entries.literal: In antiquity all eunuchs came from punished men; those mutilated by punishment could not be ranked among gentlemen and commoners, so they managed palace and temple affairs and were called 'palace women attendants.'

entries.zh: 東漢以來，宦者養子以繼世。
entries.en: From the Eastern Han dynasty on, eunuchs adopted sons to carry on their family lines.
entries.literal: From the Eastern Han onward, eunuchs adopted sons to continue their lineages.

entries.zh: 唐世，繼者皆為閹人，其初進也，性多巧慧便僻、善固恩寵，及其得志，黨比糾結不可制。
entries.en: Under the Tang, every successor was a castrated man. On first entering court they were apt to be clever, pliant, and devious, expert at holding imperial favor; once they rose to power, their factions knotted together beyond restraint.
entries.literal: In the Tang age, successors were all castrated men; when they first entered service, their natures were mostly clever, artful, and devious, skilled at securing favor, and once they gained their aims, factional cliques formed and could not be controlled.

entries.zh: 東漢以宦者亡，唐又甚焉。
entries.en: The Eastern Han fell to ruin through eunuchs, and the Tang suffered even worse.
entries.literal: The Eastern Han perished because of eunuchs, and the Tang suffered even more severely.

entries.zh: 世儒論宦者之害，如毒藥猛虎之不可拯也。
entries.en: Scholars of the age described the harm done by eunuchs as beyond remedy — like poison or a ravening tiger.
entries.literal: Confucian scholars of the age spoke of the harm of eunuchs as poison or a fierce tiger that cannot be remedied.

entries.zh: 金法置近侍局，嘗與政事，而宦者少與焉。
entries.en: Jin institutions set up the Imperial Attendants Bureau, which at times handled state affairs, yet eunuchs seldom had a role in it.
entries.literal: Under Jin law the Imperial Attendants Bureau was established and at times took part in government affairs, but eunuchs had little share in it.

entries.zh: 惟海陵時有梁珫，章宗時有梁道、李新喜幹政，二君為所誤多矣。
entries.en: Only under Emperor Hailing did Liang Chong, and under Emperor Zhangzong did Liang Dao and Li Xinxi, meddle in government — and both sovereigns were led badly astray.
entries.literal: Only under Hailing there was Liang Chong, and under Zhangzong there were Liang Dao and Li Xinxi meddling in government; both rulers were greatly misled by them.

entries.zh: 世傳梁道勸章宗納李妃後宮，金史不載梁道始末，弗得而論次之。
entries.en: Tradition holds that Liang Dao persuaded Zhangzong to take Consort Li into the harem, but the History of Jin does not record Liang Dao's full story, so his career cannot be set out here in proper sequence.
entries.literal: Popular tradition says Liang Dao urged Zhangzong to take Consort Li into the inner palace; the History of Jin does not record Liang Dao's beginning and end, so he cannot be arranged in narrative order.

entries.zh: 惟宋珪、潘守恆頗能諷諫宣、哀，時有裨益，蓋傭之佼佼、鐵之錚錚者也。
entries.en: Only Song Gui and Pan Shouheng could remonstrate with Emperors Xuanzong and Aizong with real effect, and at times they did genuine good — the finest among servants, ringing true as tempered iron.
entries.literal: Only Song Gui and Pan Shouheng were fairly able to remonstrate with the Xuanzong and Aizong emperors and at times were of benefit — outstanding among hirelings, ringing like iron.

entries.zh: 作《宦者傳》。
entries.en: Hence these biographies of eunuchs.
entries.literal: Therefore the 'Biographies of Eunuchs' was composed.

entries.zh: 太史公敘九流，述《日者》、《龜策》、《扁鵲倉公列傳》。
entries.en: Grand Historian Sima Qian surveyed the Nine Schools and wrote the biographies of day-diviners, tortoise-and-yarrow specialists, and the physicians Bian Que and Lord Cang.
entries.literal: Grand Historian Sima Qian arranged the Nine Schools and composed the 'Biographies of the Day Diviners,' 'Tortoise and Yarrow,' and 'Bian Que and Lord Cang.'

entries.zh: 劉歆校中秘書，以術數、方伎載之《七略》。
entries.en: Liu Xin collated the imperial library and placed numerology and the technical arts in his Seven Summaries.
entries.literal: Liu Xin collated the imperial secretariat books and placed numerology and technical arts in the Seven Summaries.

entries.zh: 後世史官作《方伎傳》，蓋祖其意焉。
entries.en: Later historians wrote biographies of technical masters in the same spirit.
entries.literal: Later dynasties' historians composed 'Biographies of Technical Masters,' broadly following his intent.

entries.zh: 或曰《素問》、《內經》言天道消長、氣運贏縮，假醫術，托岐黃，以傳其秘奧耳。
entries.en: Some hold that the Plain Questions and Inner Canon really speak of Heaven's waxing and waning and the ebb and flow of cosmic breath, using medicine and the names of Qi Bo and the Yellow Emperor only as vehicles for hidden doctrine.
entries.literal: Some say the Plain Questions and Inner Canon speak of the waxing and waning of Heaven's Way and the surplus and deficit of vital breath, borrowing medicine and entrusting it to Qi Bo and the Yellow Emperor merely to transmit secret profundities.

entries.zh: 秦人至以《周易》列之卜筮，斯豈易言哉！
entries.en: The Qin even filed the Book of Changes under divination — such matters are not lightly judged!
entries.literal: The people of Qin even classified the Book of Changes under divination — this is surely not easily spoken of!

entries.zh: 第古之為術，以吉凶導人而為善，後世術者，或以休咎導人為不善，古之為醫，以活人為功，後世醫者，或因以為利而誤殺人。
entries.en: In antiquity practitioners of the arts used omens to steer people toward good; later ones sometimes used fortune and misfortune to lead them astray. Ancient physicians measured their merit by lives saved; later ones sometimes chased profit and killed by mistake.
entries.literal: Only in antiquity those who practiced arts used fortune and misfortune to guide people toward good; later practitioners sometimes used omens to lead people toward evil. In antiquity physicians took saving lives as merit; later physicians sometimes pursued profit and by mistake killed people.

entries.zh: 故為政於天下，雖方伎之事，亦必慎其所職掌，而務旌別其賢否焉。
entries.en: Whoever governs the realm must therefore be careful even over technical arts, distinguishing clearly between the worthy and the unworthy.
entries.literal: Therefore in governing the realm, even in matters of technical arts one must be careful in what offices hold and strive to distinguish the worthy from the unworthy.

entries.zh: 金世，如武禎、武亢之信而不誣，劉完素、張元素之治療通變，學其術者皆師尊之，不可不記雲。
entries.en: Under the Jin, men such as Wu Zhen and Wu Kang proved trustworthy and true, while Liu Wansu and Zhang Yuansu were masters of adaptive treatment. All who learned from them revered them as teachers — and they must be recorded.
entries.literal: In the Jin age, men such as Wu Zhen and Wu Kang were faithful and not deceitful, and Liu Wansu and Zhang Yuansu were versatile in treatment; all who studied their arts honored them as teachers — they cannot go unrecorded.

entries.zh: 宣皇帝諱懿，字仲達，河內溫縣孝敬里人，姓司馬氏。
entries.en: Emperor Xuan had the personal name Yi and the courtesy name Zhongda. He came from Xiaojing Ward in Wen County, Henei Commandery, and belonged to the Sima clan.
entries.literal: Emperor Xuan's taboo name was Yi; his courtesy name was Zhongda. He was a native of Xiaojing Ward in Wen County in Henei, and his surname was Sima.

entries.zh: 其先出自帝高陽之子重黎，為夏官祝融。
entries.en: The line descended from Chongli, son of Zhuanxu, who served as Zhurong under the ancient office of Xia.
entries.literal: His ancestors traced their line to Chongli, son of Emperor Gaoyang (Zhuanxu), who held the office of Zhurong under the Xia.

entries.zh: 歷唐、虞、夏、商，世序其職。
entries.en: Across Tang, Yu, Xia, and Shang, his forebears held that post in unbroken succession.
entries.literal: Through the eras of Tang, Yu, Xia, and Shang, generation after generation they succeeded one another in that office.

entries.zh: 及周，以夏官為司馬。
entries.en: Under the Zhou, the old Xia office became the office of Sima, the marshal.
entries.literal: Under the Zhou, the Xia ministry was styled Marshal (Sima).

entries.zh: 其後程伯休父，周宣王時，以世官克平徐方，錫以官族，因而為氏。
entries.en: Later, Cheng Bo Xiufu—during King Xuan of Zhou—used his hereditary charge to crush the Xu region and received a clan designation from his title; from that the Sima surname arose.
entries.literal: Later Cheng Bo Xiufu, in the reign of King Xuan of Zhou, by virtue of his hereditary office conquered and pacified the Xu lands and was granted a clan name taken from his office; his descendants therefore took Sima as their surname.

entries.zh: 楚漢間，司馬卬為趙將，與諸侯伐秦。
entries.en: In the turmoil between Chu and Han, Sima Ang commanded troops for Zhao and marched with the alliance against Qin.
entries.literal: Between Chu and Han, Sima Ang served as a Zhao general and joined the feudal lords in attacking Qin.

entries.zh: 秦亡，立為殷王，都河內。
entries.en: After Qin collapsed he was enthroned as king of Yin with his seat at Henei.
entries.literal: When Qin fell, [Ang] was established as King of Yin and made his capital in Henei.

entries.zh: 漢以其地為郡，子孫遂家焉。
entries.en: The Han turned that territory into a commandery, and his line took root there.
entries.literal: Han converted his territory into a commandery, and his descendants settled there.

entries.zh: 自卬八世，生征西將軍鈞，字叔平。
entries.en: Eight generations down from Ang came General Who Guards the West Jun, whose courtesy name was Shuping.
entries.literal: Eight generations after Ang was born General Who Guards the West Jun, courtesy name Shuping.

entries.zh: 鈞生豫章太守量，字公度。
entries.en: Jun’s son was Liang, prefect of Yuzhang, courtesy name Gongdu.
entries.literal: Jun fathered Prefect of Yuzhang Liang, courtesy name Gongdu.

entries.zh: 量生潁川太守儁，字元異。
entries.en: Liang’s son was Jun, prefect of Yingchuan, courtesy name Yuanyi.
entries.literal: Liang fathered Prefect of Yingchuan Jun, courtesy name Yuanyi.

entries.zh: 儁生京兆尹防，字建公。
entries.en: Jun’s son was Fang, governor of Jingzhao, courtesy name Jiangong.
entries.literal: Jun fathered Governor of the Metropolitan Region Fang, courtesy name Jiangong.

entries.zh: 帝即防之第二子也。
entries.en: He was the second son of Fang.
entries.literal: The Emperor was Fang’s second son.

entries.zh: 少有奇節，聰朗多大略，博學洽聞，伏膺儒教。
entries.en: Even young he revealed unusual steadfastness—acute, far-sighted, erudite, and steeped in the Confucian canon.
entries.literal: In youth he showed uncommon integrity; he was bright and broad in strategic grasp, widely read and well informed, and devoted himself to Confucian teaching.

entries.zh: 漢末大亂，常慨然有憂天下心。
entries.en: As Han unraveled, he was repeatedly consumed by anxiety for the empire.
entries.literal: At the end of Han, when great turmoil arose, he often felt stirred with concern for the realm.

entries.zh: 南陽太守同郡楊俊名知人，[1]見帝，未弱冠，以為非常之器。
entries.en: Yang Jun of Nanyang—his fellow townsman and a celebrated judge of talent—met him before his cap-and-girdle ceremony and pronounced him a figure of rare promise.
entries.literal: Yang Jun of the same commandery, prefect of Nanyang, famed for judging men,[1] met the Emperor before his twentieth year and deemed him an extraordinary vessel.

entries.zh: 尚書清河崔琰與帝兄朗善，亦謂朗曰：「君弟聰亮明允，剛斷英特，非子所及也。」
entries.en: Cui Yan of Qinghe, who served in the Secretariat, was close to his elder brother Sima Lang and told Lang, “Your brother combines lucidity with integrity and carries an iron decisiveness—you cannot rival him.”
entries.literal: Minister Cui Yan of Qinghe was on good terms with the Emperor’s elder brother Lang and also said to Lang, “Your younger brother is clear-sighted and fair-minded, resolute and extraordinary—not someone you can match.”

entries.zh: 漢建安六年，郡舉上計掾。
entries.en: In Han’s sixth Jian’an year the commandery recommended him as clerk for the capital assessment.
entries.literal: In the sixth year of Jian’an of Han, the commandery nominated him as clerk for the annual accounts.

entries.zh: 魏武帝為司空，聞而辟之。
entries.en: Cao Cao, then minister of works, heard of him and summoned him to service.
entries.literal: Emperor Wu of Wei was Minister of Works and, hearing of him, summoned him.

entries.zh: 帝知漢運方微，不欲屈節曹氏，辭以風痹，不能起居。
entries.en: Knowing the Han house was in decline, he refused to bend himself to the Cao clan and pleaded crippling wind paralysis that kept him from rising.
entries.literal: The Emperor knew Han’s mandate was failing and did not wish to bend his integrity to the Cao house; he declined on the grounds of wind paralysis and inability to rise.

entries.zh: 魏武使人夜往密刺之，帝堅臥不動。
entries.en: Cao Cao sent someone at night to stab him secretly, but Sima Yi lay rigidly in bed and did not move.
entries.literal: Emperor Wu sent someone by night to stab him secretly; the Emperor lay rigid and did not move.

entries.zh: 及魏武為丞相，又辟為文學掾，敕行者曰：「若復盤桓，便收之。」
entries.en: When Cao Cao became Chancellor he summoned him again as literary clerk and told the courier, “If he hesitates once more, seize him.”
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu became Chancellor, he again summoned him as clerk for literature and instructed the messenger: “If he stalls again, arrest him.”

entries.zh: 帝懼而就職。
entries.en: Terrified, he accepted the appointment.
entries.literal: The Emperor, in fear, took the post.

entries.zh: 於是使與太子游處，遷黃門侍郎，轉議郎、丞相東曹屬，尋轉主簿。
entries.en: Thereafter he was assigned to attend the crown prince, promoted to Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates, transferred to Consultant and then aide in the Chancellor's Eastern Bureau, and soon made chief clerk.
entries.literal: Thereafter he was assigned to attend the crown prince, promoted to Gentleman Attendant at the Yellow Gates, transferred to Consultant and then aide in the Chancellor's Eastern Bureau, and soon made chief clerk.

entries.zh: 魏國既建，遷太子中庶子。
entries.en: Once the Wei kingdom was founded he rose to palace attendant to the heir apparent.
entries.literal: When the state of Wei was established, he was promoted to palace attendant to the heir apparent.

entries.zh: 每與大謀，輒有奇策，為太子所信重，與陳羣、吳質、朱鑠號曰四友。
entries.en: In every grand council he supplied sharp schemes; the heir relied on him and paired him with Chen Qun, Wu Zhi, and Zhu Shuo as the “Four Friends.”
entries.literal: Whenever major plans were laid he produced striking stratagems; the heir trusted and esteemed him, and with Chen Qun, Wu Zhi, and Zhu Shuo he was called the Four Friends.

entries.zh: 從討張魯，言於魏武曰：「劉備以詐力虜劉璋，蜀人未附而遠爭江陵，此機不可失也。
entries.en: On the expedition against Zhang Lu he urged Cao Cao: “Liu Bei bullied his way into Yi through trickery; the Shu populace still mistrusts him while he reaches for Jiangling—do not let this opening slip.
entries.literal: Accompanying the campaign against Zhang Lu, he said to Emperor Wu, “Liu Bei seized Liu Zhang by deceit and force; the people of Shu are not yet attached, yet he contests Jiangling from afar—this opportunity must not be missed.

entries.zh: 今若曜威漢中，益州震動，進兵臨之，勢必瓦解。
entries.en: Show strength in Hanzhong and Yi province will reel; press forward and their front will collapse.
entries.literal: If we now display our might in Hanzhong, Yizhou will be shaken; advance the army against it and it will surely crumble.

entries.zh: 因此之勢，易為功力。
entries.en: Ride that tide and the task becomes straightforward.
entries.literal: Riding this momentum, success will come easily.

entries.zh: 聖人不能違時，亦不失時矣。」
entries.en: Even the sage neither fights the moment nor lets it pass unused.”
entries.literal: The sage cannot defy the hour, yet neither does he miss it.”

entries.zh: 魏武曰：「人苦無足，既得隴右，復欲得蜀！」
entries.en: Cao Cao replied, “People are never satisfied—take Longyou and they hunger for Shu!”
entries.literal: Emperor Wu said, “Men suffer from insatiable greed—having gained Longyou, they want Shu too!”

entries.zh: 言竟不從。
entries.en: He would not take the counsel.
entries.literal: In the end he did not follow the advice.

entries.zh: 既而從討孫權，破之。
entries.en: He later joined the campaign against Sun Quan and helped rout him.
entries.literal: He then accompanied the campaign against Sun Quan and defeated him.

entries.zh: 軍還，權遣使乞降，上表稱臣，陳說天命。
entries.en: On the army’s return Sun Quan sent envoys suing for peace, presented a memorial as a vassal, and rehearsed Heaven’s mandate.
entries.literal: When the army returned, Sun Quan sent envoys begging to surrender, submitted a memorial declaring himself a subject, and expounded the mandate of Heaven.

entries.zh: 魏武帝曰：「此兒欲踞吾著爐炭上邪！」
entries.en: Cao Cao snapped, “Does that boy mean to roast me over live coals?”
entries.literal: Emperor Wu of Wei said, “Does this fellow want to seat me on coals over a furnace?”

entries.zh: 答曰：「漢運垂終，殿下十分天下而有其九，以服事之。
entries.en: He answered: “The Han flame gutters while you hold nine parts in ten yet still bow to the emperor.
entries.literal: He replied: “Han’s mandate is near its end; Your Highness holds nine-tenths of the realm yet still serves it.

entries.zh: 權之稱臣，天人之意也。
entries.en: Sun Quan’s offer to submit answers both Heaven and the human heart.
entries.literal: Sun Quan’s submission accords with the will of Heaven and men.

entries.zh: 虞、夏、殷、周不以謙讓者，畏天知命也。」
entries.en: The sage-kings of Yu, Xia, Shang, and Zhou yielded not from timidity but because they revered Heaven and accepted its mandate.”
entries.literal: Yu, Xia, Yin, and Zhou did not yield out of mere modesty—they feared Heaven and knew the mandate.”

entries.zh: 遷為軍司馬，言於魏武曰：「昔箕子陳謀，以食為首。
entries.en: Promoted army marshal, he told Cao Cao: “When Jizi advised the king, grain came first.
entries.literal: He was promoted to army marshal and said to Emperor Wu, “When Jizi presented his counsel, he put food first.

entries.zh: 今天下不耕者蓋二十餘萬，非經國遠籌也。
entries.en: Today more than two hundred thousand people are not farming; that is no long-range plan for governing the state.
entries.literal: Today perhaps two hundred thousand men do not till the soil—this is no far-reaching policy for governing the state.

entries.zh: 雖戎甲未卷，自宜且耕且守。」
entries.en: Even while armor has not yet been put away, we should farm and defend at the same time.”
entries.literal: Though armor is not yet laid aside, we should farm and defend at the same time.”

entries.zh: 魏武納之，於是務農積穀，國用豐贍。
entries.en: Cao Cao agreed; farming and granaries were stressed until state stores overflowed.
entries.literal: Emperor Wu accepted this; agriculture was emphasized and grain stored, and state supplies grew ample.

entries.zh: 帝又言荊州刺史胡脩粗暴，南鄉太守傅方驕奢，並不可居邊。
entries.en: He further warned that Hu Xiu, inspector of Jingzhou, was brutish and Fu Fang, prefect of Nanxiang, was decadent—neither belonged on the border.
entries.literal: The Emperor also said that Hu Xiu, inspector of Jingzhou, was brutal and coarse, and Fu Fang, prefect of Nanxiang, arrogant and extravagant—neither was fit to hold the frontier.

entries.zh: 魏武不之察。
entries.en: Cao Cao brushed the warning aside.
entries.literal: Emperor Wu did not heed him.

entries.zh: 及蜀將關羽圍曹仁於樊，于禁等七軍皆沒，脩、方果降羽，而仁圍甚急焉。
entries.en: When Guan Yu of Shu penned Cao Ren at Fan and Yu Jin’s seven corps vanished beneath the flood, Hu Xiu and Fu Fang duly defected to Guan Yu and the siege of Fan tightened unbearably.
entries.literal: When Shu general Guan Yu besieged Cao Ren at Fan and Yu Jin’s seven armies were drowned, Hu and Fu indeed surrendered to Guan Yu, and Ren’s siege grew desperate.

entries.zh: 魏武以荊州遺黎及屯田在潁川者逼近南寇，[2]皆欲徙之。
entries.en: Cao Cao meant to uproot the leftover households of Jingzhou and the military colonies in Yingchuan because both fronts skirted the southern enemy.
entries.literal: Emperor Wu wished to relocate the remnant people of Jingzhou and the agricultural colonies in Yingchuan because they lay close to the southern foe.

entries.zh: 帝曰：「荊楚輕脫，易動難安。
entries.en: He replied, “The Jing-Chu folk are restless—quick to bolt and slow to reassure.
entries.literal: The Emperor said, “The people of Jing-Chu are flighty—easy to stir, hard to settle.

entries.zh: 關羽新破，諸為惡者藏竄觀望。
entries.en: Guan Yu’s fall leaves malcontents skulking in the shadows, watching.
entries.literal: Guan Yu has just been defeated; those who meant harm hide and watch.

entries.zh: 今徙其善者，既傷其意，將令去者不敢復還。」
entries.en: Uproot the loyal now and you crush their hearts; refugees will never dare come home.”
entries.literal: If we now relocate the good among them, we wound their feelings and will make those who flee dare not return.”

entries.zh: 從之。
entries.en: Cao Cao relented.
entries.literal: [Emperor Wu] followed this.

entries.zh: 其後諸亡者悉復業。
entries.en: Later every exile drifted back to his fields.
entries.literal: Afterwards all who had fled resumed their occupations.

entries.zh: 是時漢帝都許昌，魏武以為近賊，欲徙河北。
entries.en: The Han emperor still sat at Xuchang; Cao Cao judged it perilously near the foe and planned to shift the court north of the river.
entries.literal: At that time the Han emperor was at Xuchang; Emperor Wu thought it too close to the enemy and wished to move the capital north of the Yellow River.

entries.zh: 帝諫曰：「禁等為水所沒，非戰守之所失，於國家大計未有所損，而便遷都，既示敵以弱，又淮沔之人大不安矣。
entries.en: He objected: “Yu Jin’s men drowned—they were not routed in the field. The empire’s strategy is intact; relocating now advertises fear and panics everyone between the Huai and the Han.
entries.literal: The Emperor remonstrated: “Yu Jin and the others were lost to water, not to defeat in battle or defense—the state’s grand plan is not yet harmed. To move the capital rashly would show weakness to the enemy and greatly unsettle the people between the Huai and the Han.

entries.zh: 孫權、劉備，外親內疏，羽之得意，權所不願也。
entries.en: Sun Quan and Liu Bei are allies in name alone; Sun Quan cannot relish Guan Yu’s triumph.
entries.literal: Sun Quan and Liu Bei are outward kin but inwardly estranged; Guan Yu’s triumph is not what Quan desires.

entries.zh: 可喻權所，令掎其後，則樊圍自解。」
entries.en: Urge Sun Quan to stab Guan Yu in the rear and the ring around Fan loosens on its own.”
entries.literal: You may instruct Quan to strike Guan Yu from behind; then the siege of Fan will lift of itself.”

entries.zh: 魏武從之。
entries.en: Cao Cao adopted the plan.
entries.literal: Emperor Wu followed this advice.

entries.zh: 權果遣將呂蒙西襲公安，拔之，羽遂為蒙所獲。
entries.en: Sun Quan dispatched Lü Meng westward against Gong’an, seized it, and Guan Yu fell into Meng’s hands.
entries.literal: Quan indeed sent general Lü Meng to raid Gong’an from the west and took it; Guan Yu was then captured by Meng.

entries.zh: 及魏武薨于洛陽，朝野危懼。
entries.en: When Cao Cao died at Luoyang, court and capital trembled.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wu died at Luoyang, court and countryside were fearful.

entries.zh: 帝綱紀喪事，內外肅然。
entries.en: He imposed discipline on the mourning rites until palace and province stood calm.
entries.literal: The Emperor directed the funeral rites; within and without there was solemn order.

entries.zh: 乃奉梓宮還鄴。
entries.en: He convoyed the royal catafalque back to Ye.
entries.literal: He then escorted the coffin back to Ye.

entries.zh: 魏文帝即位，封河津亭侯，轉丞相長史。
entries.en: When Emperor Wen of Wei ascended the throne, Sima Yi was enfeoffed as Marquis of Hejin Village and transferred to be chief clerk to the chancellor.
entries.literal: When Emperor Wen of Wei ascended the throne, Sima Yi was enfeoffed as Marquis of Hejin Village and transferred to be chief clerk to the chancellor.

entries.zh: 會孫權帥兵西過，朝議以樊、襄陽無穀，不可以禦寇。
entries.en: At the time, Sun Quan led troops westward. Court discussion held that Fan and Xiangyang had no grain and could not be used to resist the invaders.
entries.literal: At the time, Sun Quan led troops westward. Court discussion held that Fan and Xiangyang had no grain and could not be used to resist the invaders.

entries.zh: 時曹仁鎮襄陽，請召仁還宛。
entries.en: At the time Cao Ren was stationed at Xiangyang, and they requested that Ren be summoned back to Wan.
entries.literal: At the time Cao Ren was stationed at Xiangyang, and they requested that Ren be summoned back to Wan.

entries.zh: 帝曰：「孫權新破關羽，此其欲自結之時也，必不敢為患。襄陽水陸之衝，禦寇要害，不可棄也。」
entries.en: The emperor said, "Sun Quan has only just defeated Guan Yu; this is the moment when he wants to secure his own position, and he certainly will not dare become a menace. Xiangyang is a crossing point for water and land routes and a vital place for resisting invaders; it cannot be abandoned."
entries.literal: The emperor said, "Sun Quan has only just defeated Guan Yu; this is the moment when he wants to secure his own position, and he certainly will not dare become a menace. Xiangyang is a crossing point for water and land routes and a vital place for resisting invaders; it cannot be abandoned."

entries.zh: 言竟不從。
entries.en: In the end, his words were not followed.
entries.literal: In the end, his words were not followed.

entries.zh: 仁遂焚棄二城，權果不為寇，魏文悔之。
entries.en: Ren accordingly burned and abandoned the two cities. Quan indeed did not invade, and Emperor Wen of Wei regretted it.
entries.literal: Ren accordingly burned and abandoned the two cities. Quan indeed did not invade, and Emperor Wen of Wei regretted it.

entries.zh: 及魏受漢禪，以帝為尚書。
entries.en: When Wei received Han's abdication, the emperor was made minister in the Secretariat.
entries.literal: When Wei received Han's abdication, the emperor was made minister in the Secretariat.

entries.zh: 頃之，轉督軍、御史中丞，封安國鄉侯。
entries.en: Before long, he was transferred to be army supervisor and palace aide to the censor-in-chief, and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Anguo Township.
entries.literal: Before long, he was transferred to be army supervisor and palace aide to the censor-in-chief, and was enfeoffed as Marquis of Anguo Township.

entries.zh: 六年，天子復大興舟師征吳，復命帝居守，內鎮百姓，外供軍資。
entries.en: The sixth year brought another massive river expedition against Wu; again he was told to stay behind—steady the interior and provision the campaign.
entries.literal: In the sixth year (225), the Son of Heaven again raised a great fleet to campaign against Wu and again ordered the Emperor to remain as guardian—pacifying the people within and supplying the army without.

entries.zh: 臨行，詔曰：「吾深以後事為念，故以委卿。
entries.en: Before embarking he proclaimed: “I brood over what follows my reign—so I lay it in your hands.
entries.literal: On departure he issued an edict: “I think deeply on what comes after me; therefore I entrust you.

entries.zh: 曹參雖有戰功，而蕭何為重。
entries.en: Cao Shen won battles, yet Xiao He anchored the state.
entries.literal: Cao Shen had battle merit, yet Xiao He mattered more.

entries.zh: 使吾無西顧之憂，不亦可乎！」
entries.en: Free my mind from the western march—is that too much to ask!”
entries.literal: Let me have no worry over the west—is that not enough!”

entries.zh: 天子自廣陵還洛陽，詔帝曰：「吾東，撫軍當總西事；
entries.en: Returning from Guangling to Luoyang he decreed: “When I march east, the Protector commands the west;
entries.literal: When the Son of Heaven returned from Guangling to Luoyang, he issued an edict to the Emperor: “When I am east, the Protector of the Army shall oversee the west;

entries.zh: 吾西，撫軍當總東事。」
entries.en: when I march west, the Protector commands the east.”
entries.literal: when I am west, the Protector of the Army shall oversee the east.”

entries.zh: 於是帝留鎮許昌。
entries.en: So he continued to anchor Xuchang.
entries.literal: Thereupon the Emperor remained to guard Xuchang.

entries.zh: 及天子疾篤，帝與曹真、陳羣等見於崇華殿之南堂，並受顧命輔政。
entries.en: When the Son of Heaven became gravely ill, the emperor, Cao Zhen, Chen Qun, and others met him in the south hall of Chonghua Palace and together received his final charge to assist in government.
entries.literal: When the Son of Heaven became gravely ill, the emperor, Cao Zhen, Chen Qun, and others met him in the south hall of Chonghua Palace and together received his final charge to assist in government.

entries.zh: 詔太子曰：「有間此三公者，慎勿疑之。」
entries.en: He instructed the crown prince, saying, "If anyone sows discord against these three lords, be careful not to doubt them."
entries.literal: He instructed the crown prince, saying, "If anyone sows discord against these three lords, be careful not to doubt them."

entries.zh: 明帝即位，改封舞陽侯。
entries.en: When Emperor Ming ascended the throne, Sima Yi's enfeoffment was changed to Marquis of Wuyang.
entries.literal: When Emperor Ming ascended the throne, Sima Yi's enfeoffment was changed to Marquis of Wuyang.

entries.zh: 初，達與亮書曰：「宛去洛八百里，去吾一千二百里，聞吾舉事，當表上天子，比相反覆，一月間也，則吾城已固，諸軍足辦。
entries.en: Da once wrote Zhuge Liang: “Wan lies eight hundred li from Luoyang and twelve hundred from me; were I to rebel, Luoyang must memorialize the throne—round-trip paperwork eats a month; by then my walls would stand firm and my troops ready.
entries.literal: Earlier Da had written to Liang: “Wan is eight hundred li from Luoyang and twelve hundred from me; when I rise, [the court] must memorialize the Son of Heaven—by the time reports go back and forth a month will have passed; then my city will be secure and my forces ready.

entries.zh: 則吾所在深險，司馬公必不自來；
entries.en: My terrain is rugged and remote—Lord Sima will never march in person;
entries.literal: My position is deep and defensible; Lord Sima will surely not come himself;

entries.zh: 諸將來，吾無患矣。」
entries.en: if only subordinates arrive I need not worry.”
entries.literal: if only his generals come, I have nothing to fear.”

entries.zh: 及兵到，達又告亮曰：「吾舉事八日，而兵至城下，何其神速也！」
entries.en: When the army appeared Da wired Liang: “Eight days into my rising and they ring my walls—what speed!”
entries.literal: When the troops arrived, Da told Liang: “I rose eight days ago and already troops are at my walls—how swift!”

entries.zh: 上庸城三面阻水，達於城外為木柵以自固。
entries.en: Shangyong hugged water on three faces; Da threw up timber palisades beyond the walls.
entries.literal: Shangyong was bounded by water on three sides; Da built a wooden palisade outside the city to fortify himself.

entries.zh: [3]帝渡水，破其柵，直造城下。
entries.en: [3] He forded the streams, smashed the stockade, and drove to the moat.
entries.literal: [3] The Emperor crossed the water, broke the palisade, and came straight to the foot of the walls.

entries.zh: 八道攻之，旬有六日，達甥鄧賢、將李輔等開門出降。
entries.en: He assaulted along eight avenues; sixteen days later Deng Xian the nephew and general Li Fu opened the gates and capitulated.
entries.literal: He attacked from eight directions; after sixteen days Deng Xian, Da’s nephew, and general Li Fu and others opened the gates and surrendered.

entries.zh: 斬達，傳首京師。
entries.en: They beheaded Meng Da and forwarded his head to Luoyang.
entries.literal: Da was executed and his head sent to the capital.

entries.zh: 俘獲萬餘人，振旅還于宛。
entries.en: They took over ten thousand prisoners and marched back to Wan with drums beating.
entries.literal: More than ten thousand captives were taken; the army marched back to Wan in good order.

entries.zh: 乃勸農桑，禁浮費，南土悅附焉。
entries.en: He urged tillage and silk production, banned needless expense, and the south rallied to him willingly.
entries.literal: He then promoted farming and sericulture, forbade wasteful spending, and the southern lands gladly submitted.

entries.zh: 五年，天子南巡，觀兵吳疆。
entries.en: In the fifth year the emperor toured south and drilled troops along Wu’s frontier.
entries.literal: In the fifth year (224), the Son of Heaven toured south and reviewed troops on Wu’s border.

entries.zh: 帝留鎮許昌，改封向鄉侯，轉撫軍、假節，領兵五千，加給事中、錄尚書事。
entries.en: He stayed to hold Xuchang, was re-enfeoffed as marquis of Xiang township, promoted Protector of the Army with credential axe, led five thousand soldiers, and added duties as palace attendant and overseer of Secretariat business.
entries.literal: The Emperor remained to guard Xuchang, was enfeoffed as marquis of Xiang township, became Protector of the Army with ceremonial axe, commanded five thousand troops, and was given concurrent posts as attendant within the palace and recorder of Secretariat affairs.

entries.zh: 帝固辭。
entries.en: He firmly declined.
entries.literal: The Emperor firmly declined.

entries.zh: 天子曰：「吾於庶事，以夜繼晝，無須臾寧息。
entries.en: The emperor said, “I chase paperwork from dusk to dawn without a breath’s pause.
entries.literal: The Son of Heaven said, “In routine affairs I follow night with day without a moment’s rest.

entries.zh: 此非以為榮，乃分憂耳。」
entries.en: That burden is not glory—it is sharing the weight on my shoulders.”
entries.literal: This is not for honor—it is to share my burdens.”

entries.zh: 黃初二年，督軍官罷，遷侍中、尚書右僕射。
entries.en: In Huangchu’s second year the army-supervisor post was scrapped; he became palace attendant and right vice director of the Secretariat.
entries.literal: In the second year of Huangchu (221), the office of supervisor of armies was abolished; he was promoted to palace attendant and right vice director of the Secretariat.

entries.zh: 及孫權圍江夏，遣其將諸葛瑾、張霸并攻襄陽，帝督諸軍討權，走之。
entries.en: When Sun Quan invested Jiangxia and Zhuge Jin with Zhang Ba struck Xiangyang together, he led the host against Sun Quan and threw him back.
entries.literal: When Sun Quan besieged Jiangxia and sent his generals Zhuge Jin and Zhang Ba jointly to attack Xiangyang, the Emperor commanded the armies against Quan and drove him off.

entries.zh: 進擊，敗瑾，斬霸，并首級千餘。
entries.en: He pressed the pursuit, routed Zhuge Jin, slew Zhang Ba, and piled up more than a thousand heads.
entries.literal: Pressing the attack, he defeated Jin, beheaded Ba, and took over a thousand heads.

entries.zh: 遷驃騎將軍。
entries.en: He was elevated to general of the agile cavalry.
entries.literal: He was promoted to general of agile cavalry.

entries.zh: 四年，遷大將軍，加大都督、假黃鉞，與曹真伐蜀。
entries.en: Fourth year: he became Grand General and supreme commander with the yellow axe, campaigning beside Cao Zhen against Shu.
entries.literal: In the fourth year he was promoted to Grand General, invested as supreme commander-in-chief with the yellow battle-axe, and joined Cao Zhen in campaigning against Shu.

entries.zh: 帝自西城斫山開道，水陸並進，泝沔而上，至於朐䏰，拔其新豐縣。
entries.en: He hacked a route from Xicheng, drove land and river columns up the Han to Quyu, and seized Xinfeng County.
entries.literal: From Xicheng he cut roads through the mountains and advanced by land and water together, moving up the Han River as far as Quyu, where he took Xinfeng County.

entries.zh: 軍次丹口，遇雨，班師。
entries.en: They paused at Dankou until storms forced a withdrawal.
entries.literal: The army halted at Dankou; rain fell and he ordered the troops withdrawn.

entries.zh: 時邊郡新附，多無戶名，魏朝欲加隱實。
entries.en: The newly subdued border prefectures still lacked proper household rolls, and the court meant to audit them.
entries.literal: At that time the newly annexed marches often lacked registered households, and the Wei court wished to verify them thoroughly.

entries.zh: 屬帝朝於京師，天子訪之於帝。
entries.en: While he was at audience in Luoyang, the emperor took him aside for advice.
entries.literal: When the Emperor attended court in the capital, the Son of Heaven consulted him on the matter.

entries.zh: 帝對曰：「賊以密網束下，故下棄之。
entries.en: He answered: “Bandits rule through a thousand petty regulations—that is why their subjects flee.
entries.literal: The Emperor replied: “The rebels bound their subjects with a harsh net, so the people abandoned them.

entries.zh: 宜弘以大綱，則自然安樂。」
entries.en: Govern with a loose rein and calm follows without forcing it.”
entries.literal: You should rule with a broad policy; then peace will come of itself.”

entries.zh: 又問二虜宜討，何者為先？
entries.en: The sovereign then asked which foe—Wu or Shu—should come first.
entries.literal: He was also asked which of the two enemies ought to be attacked first.

entries.zh: 對曰：「吳以中國不習水戰，故敢散居東關。
entries.en: He said: “Wu gambles that we fear naval combat, so they string their lines along the eastern passes.
entries.literal: He replied: “Wu presumes that the Central Plains do not excel at river warfare, which is why they dare scatter their forces along Dongguan.

entries.zh: 凡攻敵，必扼其喉而摏其心。
entries.en: Strike always at throat and heart—that is how wars are won.
